Description
Location: Fairbanks, Alaska

Position Type: Seasonal, Full-Time (40 hrs/week)

Salary: Approximately $24/hour

Start Date: February - April 2027 

Application Deadline: October 19, 2026 

 The College of Fisheries and Ocean Sciences at University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF) and Dr. Andy Seitz research lab, invites individuals to submit a statement of interest for the position of Fisheries Technician on our hydrokinetic energy research team. Please note, this is not the formal application process but an initial step to express interest. This position is part of a study assessing the impacts of hydrokinetic turbines on fish populations in the Yukon River in Interior Alaska. The successful candidate will work as a seasonal technician in spring and summer 2027 and, upon acceptance into the graduate program at UAF, transition into a funded Master of Science program in Fisheries at UAF beginning Fall 2027.

The primary responsibilities of this position include: 1) conducting baseline research to describe the fish community in the Yukon River near the village of Galena, AK; 2) monitoring lateral distribution of down-migrating salmon using fyke nets and an inclined plane trap; 3) modeling the probability of salmon collisions with hydrokinetic energy devices; and 4) working with local stakeholders to describe community perceptions of fisheries interactions with turbines. 

Qualifications: The ideal candidate will have a B.S. in Fisheries, Ecology, Biology, or a related field (preferred); have strong quantitative skills (preferred); be respectful while working in remote, rural areas where fisheries are culturally important; be motivated, detail-oriented, and capable of working independently and as part of a team; be comfortable working in occasional harsh weather conditions and camping overnight; possess skills to operate four-wheel-drive vehicles, tow trailers, and operate boats; be able to lift up to 50 lbs.

UAF is committed to building a culturally diverse and inclusive organization. We welcome applicants to bring their unique perspectives and identities through their culture, national origin, ethnicity, race, gender, sexual orientation, veteran status, disability, age, religion and beliefs. Individuals in chronically underrepresented groups in STEM are highly encouraged to apply.

To Apply: Email the following materials to Deanna Strohm ddstrohm@alaska.edu: 1) cover letter describing your interest in the position, skills, and goals; 2) CV or resume; 3) unofficial transcripts; and 4) contact information for three references. After the initial screening, top applicants will be invited to complete a formal application through UA Careers. Additionally, candidates selected for further consideration will be required to apply to the College of Fisheries and Ocean Sciences graduate program at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.

Description
Cal Poly Humboldt’s Department of Wildlife seeks a master’s student to study barn owl nest-site selection in California almond and pistachio orchards. Fieldwork in the southern Central Valley in late spring/early summer 2027 and 2028 will involve monitoring 64 new camera-equipped nest boxes, half containing debris from previously used barn owl boxes, to test whether barn owls use social cues when selecting nest sites. The student will also help capture and age colonizing owls and fit as many as possible with GPS trackers. The position runs from January 2027 through December 2028 and pays $33,280 annually for 20 hours/week during the academic year, while also taking classes, and 40 hours/week during summer (@$26/hr). An in-state tuition waiver worth approximately $11,000/year is also included. Applicants from the 15 Western States receive the full waiver; those from other states are responsible for out-of-state tuition, currently $396/unit.

The position will also involve supervising one field technicians to assist with field work. The work is funded by the California Dept of Pesticide Regulation and will involve collaboration with Drs. Danny Karp and Roger Baldwin from UC Davis’s Dept of Wildlife, Fish, and Conservation Biology.

Required qualifications include: (a) BS in Ecology, Wildlife or related field, (b) interest in and capacity for technical aspects of camera traps and GPS tags, (c) strong quantitative skills, (d) interest in agroecology, and (e) willingness to work in hot conditions and in collaboration with private farms. Preferred qualifications include experience handling raptors, experience with statistical modeling analyses using R, and/or experience working with farmers. 

Candidates should express interest with a cover letter/statement of purpose, resume, and list of three references in an email to Matt Johnson at matt.johnson@humboldt.edu; please use the subject line OWL SOCIAL CUE MS APPLICANT. Your application statement of purpose should express interest in this position and articulate the required and any preferred qualifications. The top selected candidate will then be asked to fully apply to the Natural Resources graduate program at Cal Poly Humboldt https://cnrs.humboldt.edu/node/294. In addition to the application documents already mentioned, the full graduate school application also requires official transcripts and a $70 application fee.

Applications accepted now (Sept 2026); review of applicants begins on 30 Oct 2026; the position remains open until filled.

Contact
Matt Johnson
7072675198
mdj6@humboldt.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
I am recruiting one or more MS or PhD students to join my lab in the Department of Biology at the
University of North Dakota, with a target start of Summer/Fall 2027. This is a new lab so incoming
students will have real input into shaping its culture and research direction.

My research examines food web and trophic dynamics in freshwater ecosystems using diet, stable isotope
and other approaches, with particular interest in how climate change and disturbance (wildfire, shifting
thermal and hydrologic regimes) reshape lake and stream food webs. My own field experience spans
watersheds in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest, but I'm equally interested in students who want to
develop projects in North Dakota's own freshwater systems — prairie pothole lakes, the Red River, Devils
Lake — or Northern Minnesota’s boundary waters and prairie-to-boreal ecotone. Potential research
directions include, but are not limited to:
●Fish and invertebrate secondary production in streams, rivers, and lakes
●Trophic responses of lakes and streams to wildfire or other acute disturbances
●Climate-driven shifts in thermal regime and cascading effects on food webs
●Braided river channel production and food web dynamics
●Stable isotope and biomarker approaches to tracking energy flow in aquatic systems
●Comparative food web structure across gradients of hydrologic connectivity or land use

Students will be trained in traditional stream ecology, stable isotope methods, quantitative food web
analysis, field sampling design, statistical/programming approaches (R), and scientific writing, and will
be supported in attending and presenting at national conferences.

Qualifications
Required:
●B.S. in ecology, biology, environmental science, or a related field
●Genuine interest in freshwater ecosystems and willingness to develop independent research skills
●Ability to work both independently and collaboratively
●Willingness to conduct fieldwork in variable conditions
Preferred:
●Prior field or laboratory research experience
●Familiarity with R or another statistical/programming environment

Funding
Incoming students begin on a Department of Biology Teaching Assistantship, with a stipend of
roughly $1,888/month (MS) or $2,388/month (PhD), tuition waiver, and health insurance.
Transition to a Research Assistantship is anticipated pending success of pending grant proposals.

To Apply
Interested applicants should submit the following as a single PDF to matthew.dunkle@und.edu with the
email subject line “GA Position (Last Name)”:
1. A brief cover letter (1 page) describing your research interests, relevant experience, and career
goals
2. A CV or resume
3. Contact information for three references
Considering applications on a rolling basis until January 31, 2027. Formal application to the UND
Biology graduate program is a separate step, due February 15 — happy to discuss timing with any
interested applicant.
Contact
Dr. Matt Dunkle Department of Biology, University of North Dakota matthew.dunkle@und.edu
Contact
Matthew R. Dunkle
matthew.dunkle@und.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
The Environmental Psychology Innovation Center (EPIC) in the Biology Department at University of Miami (Go Canes!) is recruiting a graduate student to begin January or August 2027. Led by Dr. Delia Shelton, one project is focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying cadmium toxicity. The second project involves understanding the transgenerational impact of fire-related contaminants on firefighter health and contaminant induced pre- and post-zygotic barriers to reproduction. Individuals with experience in RNA seq, qRT-PCR, bisulfite sequencing, TUNEL staining, ELISAS, histopathology, ICP-MS, GC-MS, LC-MS, and oxidative stress are encouraged to apply.  Read more about our work at deliashelton.com and Firefighter Cancer Initiative . 
 
By joining the lab the researcher will be a member of a vibrant, diverse, and inclusive research community with opportunities to lead and collaborate on new research directions. They will contribute to publications, grant proposals, animal husbandry, lab maintenance and collaborative projects. The lab is housed in a palm tree-lined building nested in a cosmopolitan city with world- class arts, entertainment and beaches, Miami, Florida, USA and is supported by NIH grant and a generous startup package. Applicants from marginalized identities, and those with interest in animal behavior, genetics and toxicology are especially encouraged to apply.

The student would be supported by teaching and research assistantships. In Biology, graduate assistantship includes a stipend of at least $4,000 per month, health benefits, and a tuition/fee waiver.

If interested, please complete EPIC Graduate Student Intake Form (https://forms.gle/q4CgWdJXAWfrDPfS8) and e-mail Dr. Delia Shelton (dshelton@miami.edu) a single PDF containing (1) a statement of interest, (2) a CV, and (3) contact information for three references. I will begin reviewing candidate applications immediately and ultimately invite selected applicants to apply to the department. The department’s application deadline is 1 December 2026. 

Contact
Delia Shelton

Description
Dr. Alison O’Dowd (https://www.humboldt.edu/environmental-science-and-management/alison-odowd) at Cal Poly Humboldt seeks applications for highly motivated students interested in pursuing graduate school in the Environmental Science & Management option of the Natural Resources Graduate Program (https://www.humboldt.edu/cnrs/graduate-programs/natural-resources). Students with an interest in estuarine invertebrates, aquatic food webs, bioenergetics models, and invertebrates as food resources for juvenile salmonids are particularly encouraged to apply.

Project Summary
The objective of this research is to understand the impact of a restoration project in the Eel River Estuary (at Cannibal Island in Northern California) on rearing habitat and landscape-scale growth potential for juvenile salmonids and other native fish species that inhabit the site. To do this, we will quantify the changes in rearing habitat (i.e., area, water quality characteristics, and invertebrate biomass availability) and potential bioenergetic differences (derived from observed differences in invertebrate biomass) for juvenile salmonids (Chinook, Coho) and other fish in the assemblage. The proposed approach is to collect pre- and post- restoration food web, water quality, and physical habitat data, stage and velocity at monthly intervals, in the restoration area and a nearby control site, during periods of key estuary rearing for juvenile salmonids (e.g. December-August). These data can be evaluated as meaningful stand-alone metrics (e.g. changes in invertebrate density and biomass, water quality and physical habitat) and integrated into a bioenergetics model to predict changes on landscape scale productivity (e.g. joules of fish growth potential per area per time). We will also explore the role of Cannibal Island as a producer and exporter of food to adjacent foraging habitat in the North Bay of the Eel River Estuary pre- and post-restoration construction. 

This graduate research project will seek to understand the invertebrate responses post-restoration to assess food resources for out-migrating juvenile salmonids and other fish. Collection and identification of estuarine invertebrates, building a bioenergetics model, and interpretation of data will be the primary tasks associated with this project.

Assistantship
·         Compensation for two years to cover living expenses and tuition ($24,000/year)
·         Project-related expenses (travel to field sites, equipment, etc.) will be covered
·         Funding to present graduate research at a professional conference

The second year of funding is conditional based on student academic standing and project progress. Program start date is August 2027.

Teaching Assistant (TA) positions with a tuition waiver may be available to qualified candidates.

Requirements
Strong applicants will have:
-          An undergraduate degree in Entomology, Zoology, Ecology, Environmental Science, Biology, Fisheries, Watershed Science, or related field
-          An undergraduate GPA of 3.0 or above
-          University-level courses in disciplines such as: ecology, fisheries, entomology, aquatic ecology, ecological restoration, and/or statistics
-          Demonstrated experience working in aquatic habitats (such as tidal sloughs, estuaries, rivers, streams, lakes) and with associated field equipment
-          Demonstrated experience sorting and identifying aquatic invertebrates
-          Demonstrated experience managing others in a laboratory setting
-          Ability to drive to field sites
-          An interest in publishing research findings in a scientific journal

To Apply:

Position Description: 

The School of Renewable Natural Resources at Louisiana State University Agricultural Center is seeking applicants for one M.S. assistantships starting as early as January or May 2026, depending on candidate availability. The assistantship is half-time (20 hours/week) and includes a 12-month stipend of $28,000/year (MS), full tuition coverage, graduate fee support, and 75% graduate student health care coverage.

Project: 

The selected student will join the LSU AgCenter Aquaculture Resilience & Conservation (ARC) Lab led by Dr. Kaelyn Fogelman and contribute to a Louisiana Sea Grant funded project examining the effects of environmental factors such as high temperature, low DO, disease, and invasive species on crawfish catchability, movement, behavior, post-harvest survival, and yield in commercial production systems. This applied research project aims to generate science-based recommendations that improve production efficiency, animal welfare, and producer profitability within Louisiana's crawfish industry.

Research activities will include both field- and pond-based investigations conducted at the LSU AgCenter Aquaculture Research Station and collaborating commercial farms. The student will be responsible for collecting and analyzing water quality and environmental data, assessing crawfish movement and behavior, evaluating harvest and catchability metrics, and conducting post-harvest survival experiments. Opportunities will also exist to participate in pond management activities, engage directly with crawfish producers, and contribute to extension and outreach products developed from the project.

Students will gain training in experimental design, aquaculture production systems, aquatic animal husbandry, data analysis, and science communication. The project will involve close collaboration with industry stakeholders, Louisiana Sea Grant personnel, and LSU AgCenter researchers, providing opportunities to develop both research and professional skills relevant to careers in aquaculture, fisheries, natural resource management, and applied agricultural sciences.

Preference will be given to highly motivated students with backgrounds or strong interests in aquaculture, fisheries, ecology, animal behavior, environmental sciences, biology, or related disciplines. Successful applicants should be comfortable working outdoors in all weather conditions, collecting field data, handling live aquatic animals, and collaborating with producers and diverse stakeholder groups. Strong organizational skills, independence, initiative, and a willingness to engage in both research and extension activities are highly desirable.

The position will remain open until a qualified candidate is selected. Review of applications will begin October 15th, 2026, with interviews beginning immediately.

Fellowship summary

The Canadian Organization for Tropical Education and Rainforest Conservation (COTERC) is seeking a passionate, driven conservation leader to oversee and advance cutting-edge research projects in Costa Rica. This year-long fellowship (with the potential to extend) offers a rare chance to gain fantastic leadership experience at the heart of tropical field research — ideally starting in December 2026/January 2027.

The opportunity

For over three decades, COTERC, a Canadian not-for-profit, has trained more than 2,500 emerging researchers at its Caribbean coast biological station, shaping conservation careers across the globe. Now, as we take on management of a second station in the breathtaking Costa Rican cloud forest, we are entering a pivotal new chapter — one where the successful candidate will help shape a bold research agenda that spans rainforest to cloud forest.

This fellowship is more than a field job. It’s an opportunity to lead research that matters, mentor the next generation of conservationists, and turn data into action that safeguards biodiversity. Working primarily at Caño Palma Biological Station (CPBS) and making regular expeditions into the cloud forest, you’ll gain hands-on experience that opens doors to senior-level roles in global conservation.

Who would make a great fellow?

A well-read conservationist, comfortable applying common statistical approaches

Minimum of a Masters or PhD in biology, ecology, or other related subject, with thesis development and research component (this is essential). 
Knowledge/familiarity with Neotropical biology/ecology. 
Working knowledge and competence with common statistical approaches and tools (R preferred). 

A leader that is easygoing, but able to manage young researchers

Experience undertaking fieldwork in challenging conditions (tropics preferred). 
Record of coordinating volunteers, student groups, or independent researchers. 
Interest in mentoring long-term students on individual research projects. 

An excellent communicator

Fluency in English and proficiency (at minimum) in spoken and written Spanish (all official documents and meetings are in Spanish). 
Experience identifying trends and writing research reports to change the behaviour of external parties. 
Experience living in close quarters, with well-developed conflict resolution skills. 

IMPORTANT! We don’t expect the Research Supervisor to meet every single competency — we encourage you to apply and acknowledge gaps in knowledge or experience.  

What will the fellow do?

As Research Supervisor, you’ll play a central role in shaping COTERC’s scientific agenda — from coordinating long-term monitoring at Caño Palma to pioneering new projects in the cloud forest. You’ll mentor and train interns and volunteers, guiding them through the rigours of field research while ensuring data integrity and safety standards. Beyond the station, you’ll engage with local communities and government agencies, turning research into action that advances conservation goals. Your work will contribute directly to applied reports, peer-reviewed publications, and the sustainable management of one of the world’s most biodiverse regions.

Coordinate long-term monitoring projects at CPBS (for a list of projects and relevant publications, see www.coterc.org) 
Train and supervise interns and volunteers on data collection across research projects. 
Develop new projects in line with COTERC’s evolving research agenda. 
Contribute to species conservation and area management through the production of applied reports and peer-reviewed papers. 
Work with local communities and government agencies to promote conservation practices. 
Oversee the management of project data, supported by the Director of Data Integrity. 
Support the Station Manager in the management of the site, ensuring health and safety policies are followed by all. 

What can we offer the fellow?

Full room and board at Caño Palma Biological Station.
$600/month stipend. 
$200 bonus every three months.
$1,000 bonus at the successful completion of 1 year contract.

Most importantly, you’ll gain unparalleled experience leading research and conservation efforts in two extraordinary ecosystems. This is a stepping-stone into senior roles across academia, NGOs, and global conservation leadership.

How to apply

Send your application (cover letter, CV, and 2–3 professional references — no more than 3 pages total 11pt font) to applications@coterc.org    

Application review and interviews begin immediately — we encourage you to apply as soon as possible.

For more about COTERC and our work, visit:

🌐 www.coterc.org

applications@coterc.org (preferred contact method)

 Position Title: Ph.D. Graduate Assistantship – Population Dynamics of North Pacific Albatrosses

Position Description: We are seeking a highly motivated Ph.D. student to pursue research that bridges seabird ecology, demographic modeling, and wildlife conservation. The successful candidate will leverage extensive long-term datasets to understand the intrinsic and extrinsic factors driving populations of two species of North Pacific albatrosses – Laysan Albatross (Mōlī) and Black-footed Albatross (Ka‘upu). The research will primarily focus on breeding colonies at Midway Atoll, with potential expansion to include populations on other islands. This project has a strong quantitative focus. The core of the research involves the development of advanced demographic models, including Integrated Population Models, to understand how local and broad-scale environmental factors and fisheries affect population status, vital rates, and demographic trends. However, the student will have significant latitude to co-develop specific research questions and analytical approaches. The student may have the opportunity (contingent upon availability of funds) to participate in field deployments to the Pacific to assist with ongoing monitoring efforts and collect targeted field data in support of their specific project objectives. The successful applicant will be expected to publish their research in peer-reviewed scientific journals and present their findings at scientific conferences. This is a highly collaborative initiative, and the student will work closely with a diverse team of researchers, field biologists, and wildlife managers, including partners at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). The successful candidate will pursue a Ph.D. degree in Wildlife and Rangeland Sciences with the Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute and Department of Rangeland and Wildlife Sciences, Texas A&M University-Kingsville. 

Required Qualifications: 
M.S. in Wildlife Science, Ecology, Statistics, or closely related field from an accredited university.
Strong quantitative and problem-solving skills, with experience in ecological modeling and statistical computing.
Excellent written and verbal communication skills, including the ability to engage with diverse audiences (scientists, wildlife managers, and the public).
Strong work ethic with the ability to work both independently and collaboratively within a research team.

Preferred Qualifications:
Demonstrated record of applied ecological research through peer-reviewed publications, presentations, or other scholarly activities.
Experience with demographic modeling within Bayesian frameworks (e.g., JAGS, Nimble).
Experience with geospatial technologies (e.g., GIS) and remote sensing data products (e.g., climate and oceanographic data).
Knowledge of seabird ecology or avian population dynamics
Experience conducting basic field ecology.

Description
With support from Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks, the University of Montana Fish and Wildlife Genomics Lab is recruiting a PhD student that will focus their efforts on several outstanding questions concerning hybridization between native cutthroat trout and introduced rainbow trout.  Conservation geneticists and fisheries managers in the state of Montana have been focused on describing, monitoring, understanding, and addressing hybridization between native cutthroat trout and rainbow trout for 50 years. Indeed, rainbow trout hybridization is often considered the primary threat to native cutthroat trout in Montana (and beyond).  However, long-term and spatially extensive data collections are beginning to reveal widely varying patterns of hybridization across space, and divergent changes in hybridization through time.  This project will use multiple sources of information to modernize our understanding of the threat of non-native hybridization for cutthroat trout conservation.  The ultimate goal of this project is to leverage various existing resources, including what is likely the world’s most extensive hybridization monitoring program, to better identify what management strategies will be most appropriate for cutthroat trout across Montana.    

This project includes two collaborative parts: (1) a post-doctoral student will focus on potential genomic mechanisms (e.g., incompatibilities) that may explain observed differences in hybridization across the state; and (2) the PhD project being advertised here will use long-term, spatially extensive data to better describe hybridization dynamics, and the potential factors that may explain heterogenous hybridization outcomes.  There are nearly 50 years of genetic data describing the extent of rainbow trout hybridization in cutthroat trout populations in Montana, including more than 100,000 individually genotyped fish.  These foundational monitoring data provide a remarkable opportunity to better describe both spatial and temporal patterns of hybridization across all cold-water habitats in the state over decades.  Specific research questions include (but are not limited to):

1.     How has the extent of rainbow trout hybridization changed across different watersheds in Montana?  

2.     Do spatial and temporal changes (increases) in rainbow trout hybridization match expectations based on abundance and distribution of rainbow trout, environmental conditions, or random mating?

3.     How common is genomic extinction, and what landscape features (e.g., isolation vs. connectivity) are associated with genomic extinction across space and time?

4.     Can spatial and temporal changes in hybridization be explained by genomic incompatibilities described/identified with genomic results? (in collaboration with post-doc)

Ultimately, these questions (and other related questions) will be used, along with genomic analyses above, to better identify the mechanisms that promote or resist rainbow trout hybridization across WCT and YCT populations in Montana.  Overall, this work will be used to directly identify those geographic regions (or environmental or genomic conditions) that are most susceptible and to rainbow trout hybridization, and in contrast, those that appear most resilient.  In so doing, this project will help biologists and managers more accurately assess risk across the wide variety of environmental conditions and intrinsic genetic/genomic variability found in cutthroat trout, both within and between species.  While the project clearly has a defined conservation focus, the overall topic and the unprecedented data set leaves opportunity to directly address key questions in the broader fields of population genetics and evolutionary ecology.

The ideal candidate for this position will have a solid understanding of population genetics, but equally importantly, experience with (or strong desire to learn) modern statistical approaches to data analysis (e.g., generalized mixed modeling, Bayesian modeling, etc.), and data generation (e.g., environmental data). We anticipate graduate opportunities for 1-2 different research projects related to (1) fish passage around lock and dam structures in large rivers, (2) movement ecology of fishes in Lake Michigan, and (3) linking landscape use with the abundance of river fishes. ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), located in Peoria, Illinois.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

The Functional Foods Research (FFR) unit in Peoria, Illinois aims at developing bioactive food ingredients that provide health benefits; and creating value-added food and nonfood products from low value agricultural resources. Scientists at FFR develop new processing, chemical, physical, and enzymatic technologies to modify food plants and enhance the use and performance of agricultural materials.

Research Project: The ORISE participant will be a part of a collaborative research initiative focused on the processing and food applications of proteins derived from plant sources such as alfalfa and legumes. Through this appointment, the participant will gain firsthand experience in how interdisciplinary scientific approaches are used to address real-world challenges in the food industry. The participant will collaborate with chemists, material scientists, plant scientists, and food engineers to build a comprehensive understanding of the utilization of oils, proteins, and phytochemicals from major and emerging U.S. crops. The participant will have access to a state-of-the-art pilot plant for seed and food processing, along with advanced analytical instrumentation such as HPLC, texture analyzers, FT-IR spectrometers, zeta potential and particle size analyzers, differential scanning calorimeters, and supercritical CO2 extractors. Hands-on training will be provided in the characterization of plant proteins, including assessment of secondary structure, surface charge and hydrophobicity, thermal properties, digestibility, texture profile, and other key techno-functional properties.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, the participant will learn to: develop and optimize procedures for extracting plant proteins with high purity, improved color, and desirable sensory attributes; conduct analyses of the structural, nutritional, and functional properties of extracted plant proteins; characterize interactions between plant proteins and co-factors, including phenolics and volatile flavor compounds; and evaluate the effects of pre-harvest factors (e.g., light exposure) and post-harvest treatments (e.g., hydrothermal processing) on protein structure and functionality.

ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

This appointment is supported by the USDA-ARS barley and oat research project in Aberdeen which goals are to enhance barley and oat productivity, quality, and stress resilience by combing traditional, molecular, and genomics methods. You will collaborate with other scientists in the unit and other institutes to develop genetic, genomic and molecular resources for  for supporting the barley and oat research.

Research Project: You will be involved with one of the two research projects: I. Barley genetics and genomics and II. Barley and oat molecular biology. For the first project, you will help conduct genetic analysis of resistance to stripe rust and hessian fly in barley and map the key genes or QTLs related to barley disease and pest resistance or other interesting traits. You will also assist in performing genome-wide association studies to identify genomic regions or candidate genes associated with disease resistance and grain quality in wild and cultivated barley populations. In addition, you will also participate in the collaborative wild barley genomics project and characterize useful genes in wild barley species. For the second project, you will contribute to cloning the genes controlling stripe rust resistance and grain quality in barley, investigating the molecular functions of the candidate genes and validating the gene functions with transformation and molecular experiments. Lastly, you will assist in analyzing the gene-edited plants to improve grain quality in barley and oat. 

Learning Objectives: You will receive training in plant genetics and breeding, plant genomics, molecular biology and gene editing, and will gaining experience collaborating with national and international scientists on plant pathology, bioinformatics, comparative evolution and other areas. You will also have opportunities to attend scientific conferences for presenting the research results and establish collaborative networks. Additionally, you will get a chance to learn barley and oat molecular biology and understand the needs of the stakeholders. Lastly, you gain skills relating to writing manuscripts, book chapters, project reports and presenting research at scientific conferences.

  Job Description                                                                                                                                                                       

The Department of Forestry in the College of Forest Resources and the Forest and Wildlife Research Center at Mississippi State University is seeking applicants for a funded M.S. assistantship to examine the professional readiness of forestry graduates and the competency needs of employers across public, private, and non-profit natural resource sectors. The student will be advised by Dr. Arun Regmi and will join the social dimensions research program in the Department of Forestry.
 
This research will investigate how existing educational experiences prepare students for careers in the field and evaluate employer expectations for entry-level professionals. By engaging recent graduates, employers, and other stakeholders, the project will identify areas of alignment and potential gaps between educational preparation and professional competency needs. Description
The Wisely Lab in the University of Florida Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation is recruiting a Ph.D. student to join a multidisciplinary project developing innovative approaches for surveillance of feral swine and African swine fever virus (ASFV).

The project uses mosquito bloodmeals as biological samples of free-ranging feral swine, an approach known as exogenous xenosurveillance. By treating blood-fed mosquitoes as “flying syringes,” the research team will evaluate whether mosquito bloodmeals can be used to detect feral swine, genetically identify individual animals, estimate population abundance, and support pathogen surveillance.


Position responsibilities

The Ph.D. student will take a leading role in the field ecology and quantitative components of the project. Responsibilities will include:

·         Coordinating deployment and sampling of camera traps and mosquito capture systems across wet and dry seasons.

·         Supervising and mentoring undergraduate researchers participating in field and laboratory activities.

·         Working with project collaborators to process mosquito bloodmeals and generate genetic data for individual identification of feral swine.

·         Developing genetic mark-recapture models to estimate feral swine abundance from mosquito-derived host DNA.

·         AND/OR

·         Developing occupancy/detection models to compare the effectiveness of mosquito-based surveillance and conventional camera trapping.

The student will be co-advised by Dr. Samantha Wisely, a wildlife disease ecologist in UF's Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, and Dr. Nathan Burkett-Cadena, a vector-borne disease ecologist at the UF Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory. The student will also collaborate closely with Dr. Tim Smyser of the USDA APHIS Wildlife Services National Feral Swine Damage Management Program on genomic approaches for individual identification of feral swine. The student will have the opportunity to also interact with Dr. Amy Vittor from the College of Medicine on serological assay development. 

An important feature of the project is the integration of research with agricultural biosecurity education. The successful candidate will work closely with a Ph.D. student specializing in science communication/agricultural education, sharing field experiences, data and scientific expertise that will inform educational materials, microcredentials and a graduate learning module in genetic mark-recapture. The science communications Ph.D. student, mentored by Dr. Grady Roberts, will lead development of the educational products; this position will contribute scientific content and collaborate on their development but will not lead the project's education component.


Minimum qualifications

Applicants should have:

·         A bachelor's or master's degree in wildlife ecology, ecology, entomology, biology, quantitative ecology, disease ecology, or a related field.

·         Previous experience conducting ecological field research.

·         Demonstrated interest in wildlife population ecology, wildlife disease, quantitative ecology, or wildlife surveillance.

·         Experience with, or strong interest in learning, population modeling and statistical analysis in R.

·         Ability and willingness to conduct extended fieldwork under hot, humid and physically demanding Florida conditions.

·         Strong organizational, written communication and teamwork skills.

·         Ability to work independently while contributing effectively to a highly interdisciplinary research team.

Experience with camera trapping, mosquito or other arthropod sampling, molecular ecology/genetics, occupancy modeling, capture-recapture analysis, or supervision of field crews is desirable but not required.


Research environment

The student will join a collaborative team spanning wildlife disease ecology, entomology, genomics, infectious disease and agricultural education, with collaborators at the University of Florida and USDA APHIS Wildlife Services. The project provides an unusual opportunity for a doctoral student to integrate intensive field ecology with molecular tools and quantitative population modeling while conducting research with direct application to wildlife management and U.S. agricultural biosecurity. 

Location: University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, with substantial fieldwork throughout Florida.
Degree: Ph.D. in Wildlife Ecology and Conservation
Advisor: Wisely, with co-advising by Nathan Burkett-Cadena

This USDA AFRI funded graduate assistanceship has four years of funding and would begin in May of 2027. Please send a cv and cover letter to Samantha Wisely at wiselylab@ifas.ufl.edu by November 15, 2026.
 
 

Contact
Samantha M Wisely
3528460645
wisely@ufl.edu (preferred contact method)

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS delivers cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence. 

ARS’s SCINet/Artificial Intelligence (AI) Center of Excellence Research Participation Program offers research opportunities to motivated postdoctoral fellows interested in solving agriculture-related problems at a range of spatial and temporal scales, from the genome to the continent, and sub-daily to evolutionary time scales. One of the goals of the SCINet Initiative is to develop and apply new technologies, including AI and machine learning (ML), to help solve complex agricultural problems that also depend on collaboration across scientific disciplines and geographic locations. In addition, many of these technologies rely on the synthesis, integration, and analysis of large, diverse datasets that benefit from high-performance computing (HPC). The objective of these fellowships is to facilitate cross-disciplinary, cross-location research through collaborative research on problems of interest to each applicant and amenable to or requiring HPC resources. Training will be provided in data science, scientific computing, AI/ML, and related topics as needed for the fellow to complete their research. Additional funds are available for supplies and travel essential for the fellow's research. 

Research Project: Throughout the course of this research project, you will have the opportunity to gain experience in and learn about unoccupied aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery collection and processing, deep learning methods, and rangeland vegetation communities in Oregon and Idaho as part of an interdisciplinary team including researchers in plant ecology, remote sensing, and computer science. 

UAV imagery and increasingly sophisticated and targeted AI algorithms can estimate forage quality, biodiversity, and the abundance of individual plant species of interest, like invasives, across broad areas (~1 – 100 ha). Under the guidance of a mentor, you will participate in a project focused on (1) applying and helping to improve upon an existing AI pipeline to classify rangeland plant species, and (2) using transfer learning to adapt deep learning models for imagery analysis to varying UAV sensors and conditions. These techniques will allow you to identify and pursue researching a range of ecological questions related to community ecology, invasive species, pollinator floral resources, restoration, and wildfire burn severity. 

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will learn about (1) geospatial processing and ML/AI methods and (2) how to contribute to SCINet and the ARS AI Center of Excellence community by developing and publishing workflows and code repositories for open-source software related to UAV imagery processing and ecological community dynamics. You will also have the opportunity to take on-line courses in scientific topics, such as R, Python, and statistics, and to learn collaboration and leadership skills through workshop and group experience. 

USDA-ARS Mentor: If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact Peter Olsoy, peter.olsoy@usda.gov

Description
 ARS Office/Lab and Location: A postdoctoral research opportunity is available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), Eastern Regional Research Center (ERRC) located in Wyndmoor, Pennsylvania.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS delivers cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence. 

ARS’s SCINet/Artificial Intelligence (AI) Center of Excellence Research Participation Program offers research opportunities to motivated postdoctoral fellows interested in solving agriculture-related problems at a range of spatial and temporal scales, from the genome to the continent, and sub-daily to evolutionary time scales. One of the goals of the SCINet Initiative is to develop and apply new technologies, including AI and machine learning (ML), to help solve complex agricultural problems that also depend on collaboration across scientific disciplines and geographic locations. In addition, many of these technologies rely on the synthesis, integration, and analysis of large, diverse datasets that benefit from high-performance computing (HPC). The objective of these fellowships is to facilitate cross-disciplinary, cross-location research through collaborative research on problems of interest to each applicant and amenable to or requiring HPC resources. Training will be provided in data science, scientific computing, AI/ML, and related topics as needed for the fellow to complete their research. Additional funds are available for supplies and travel essential for the fellow's research. 

Research Project: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will conduct research on non-targeted analysis of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in food, food contact materials, and agricultural samples. Throughout the course of this research project, you will gain experience in developing machine learning tools for the identification and analysis of unknown PFAS, supporting agricultural research and advancing the ARS mission. The project will involve compiling high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) databases for PFAS, creating machine learning models trained on high-quality standards across diverse PFAS classes, and validating prediction accuracy and error rates. These tools will then be applied to real-world agricultural samples to detect previously unreported PFAS, contributing to enhanced food safety.  

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will learn to conduct research in the food safety arena, develop novel advanced analytical techniques for food safety monitoring, and evaluate the analytical performance aspects of different types of advanced instrumentation. Additionally, you will learn about a wide range of activities related to organizational and operational planning and science communication in support of SCINet and the ARS AI Center of Excellence (AI-COE). You will also have the opportunity to take online courses in scientific topics, such as R, Python, and statistics, and to learn collaboration and leadership skills through workshop and group experience.  

USDA-ARS Mentor: If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact Yelena Sapozhnikova, ARS/USDA, Yelena.sapozhnikova@usda.gov.

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: 2027. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors. 

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year but may be renewed for a second year upon recommendation of the mentor and ARS. 

Level of Participation: The appointment is full-time. 

Participant Stipend: The participant(s) will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience. The current stipend range for this opportunity is $100,000 - $110,000/year plus a supplement to offset health insurance costs. Funding is also available to help offset relocation costs, if applicable. 

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE. 

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.ARS.SCINet@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a doctoral degree in the one of the relevant fields. 

Preferred skills:  

Advanced knowledge of high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) 
Experience in non-targeted analysis, data handling and analysis, including proficiency in R and Python 
Strong problem-solving skills 
Experience developing, testing, and refining machine learning models  
Excellent written and oral communication skills 
Experience with publishing in peer-reviewed journals

Description
I am looking for a new doctoral student in my Aquatic Ecology lab for Fall 2027 (North Miami, FL). I am looking for a curious independent thinker who is honest, hard-working and motivated to study populations or communities in aquatic ecosystems, specifically in wetlands. The PhD project may involve use of long-term data collected on federal and state-funded monitoring projects.  Dissertation topics are partly at the discretion of the student, but some aspect should involve population ecology, invasive fish ecology or trophic interactions of aquatic animals or wading birds in the context of wetland environmental variation (droughts, floods, nutrients).  The immediate context of our work is the Everglades wetland of southern Florida.  (Current PhD students are studying population dynamics and predator-prey interactions in food webs of temporary wetlands).
 The position will be supported each year with a combination of research and teaching assistantship (annual stipend of $30,625 plus a tuition waiver and health benefits) with opportunities to apply for fellowships in later years.   It may be possible that the position could start earlier in the summer (May-June) as a technician before matriculation. 
    Qualifications: 
The positions require a bachelor’s degree in biology plus extensive research experience or a completed MS degree in a related field.  A demonstrated strong work ethic and the ability to conduct field work and data analyses will both be important. The student will become part of a large lab (students, postdocs and technicians) and therefore having the ability to both work in a team and independently will be required. Previous scientific writing experience is important. An MS degree and prior research experience with ecology and/or work in wetlands are desirable.  Minimum academic qualifications include an undergraduate GPA > 3.0 three letters of recommendation. A GRE is helpful, but not required. A valid driver's license is required.  
 Interested students should send their materials to Dr. Nathan Dorn (ndorn@fiu.edu) before officially applying to the PhD program at FIU (https://case.fiu.edu/biology/phd-in-biology/admissions/index.html).  
 Please send a cover letter explaining your research interest, background/suitability and your career goals, and what about my lab is a good fit for your research interest.  Also send a resume or CV (including any degrees/scores) and contact information for 3 professional references (professors, supervisors or employers) before December 4, 2026. Review of applications (by Dr. Dorn) will begin in mid-November. Applicants of minority status and underserved groups are encouraged to apply.  
Contact
Nathan Dorn
3059194234
ndorn@fiu.edu (preferred contact method)

Job Description
Tenure-track faculty position (open-rank tenure track position) with the Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute (CKWRI) in the Department of Rangeland and Wildlife Sciences (RWSC) and Dick and Mary Lewis Kleberg College of Agriculture and Natural Resources at Texas A&M University-Kingsville. This endowed chair position includes expectations of developing an extramurally funded research program focused on quail ecology and management (75%), teaching 1 graduate and 1 undergraduate level course (25%), and will be a 9-month appointment with potential for summer salary. We seek an accomplished scholar to lead an impactful and dynamic quail and upland gamebird research program, contribute to undergraduate and graduate student academic growth using the best practices in teaching and mentorship, and extend results to stakeholders, society, and the scientific community. The Glassell Chair in Quail Research will work closely with faculty including other upland gamebird scientists at CKWRI and will have access to a variety of resources to support quail research. Initial salary shall be commensurate with qualifications and experience.

Essential Duties and Responsibilities
Research 
Develop and lead an impactful, dynamic, and extramurally funded quail and upland gamebird research program, with a focus in Texas commensurate with a 75% research appointment.
Engage in scholarly activities appropriate to the discipline, contributing to the university’s research mission.

Teaching
 Teach 1 graduate-level and 1 undergraduate-level course annually 
Maintain high standards of teaching effectiveness and student engagement.

Service
 Mentor graduate and undergraduate students in research and professional development.
Engage in professional service within the Department, College, and University.

Qualifications
Applicants must have earned a Ph.D. in ecology, wildlife science, rangeland science, or closely related field from an accredited university. 
Evidence of innovative and applied research within wildlife or rangeland sciences, quail/upland gamebird management and ecology, ornithology, or ecology demonstrated by a record of producing manuscripts, presentations, and other scholarly materials. 
A dedication to teaching and the ability to instruct courses in wildlife and rangeland ecology and management, incorporating new technologies and teaching techniques into classes. Applicants must have successfully completed a minimum of 18 graduate-level hours in wildlife and rangeland science or similar disciplines related to ecosystem management. 
Demonstrated potential to attract extramural funding. 
Demonstrated ability to communicate with students, professionals, lay audiences, and other scientists. 

Preferred Qualifications
Experience conducting research on upland gamebirds in working landscapes. 
Strong quantitative skills. 
Demonstrated ability to foster and sustain positive, working relationships with private landowners, other faculty, students, and state, federal, tribal, and private natural resource organizations. 
Postdoctoral experience which may include University teaching and research. 

Knowledge, Skills and Abilities
 Strong ability to communicate research findings through peer-reviewed publications, presentations, and via media contributions 
Ability to build and sustain a nationally recognized research program through grantsmanship, graduate student recruitment and mentoring, and a strong professional presence. 
Ability to engage with diverse stakeholders (e.g., private landowners, agency personnel) in South Texas and beyond 
Ability to positively and professionally interact with students, faculty, and staff 
Skilled in using various learning strategies to maintain teaching effectiveness 
Ability to advise, mentor, and guide students to promote student success 

Additional Information
 This position is security sensitive 
This position will require export-control authorization prior to starting employment. 
This position requires compliance with state and federal laws/codes and Texas A&M University System/TAMU policies, regulations, rules and procedures 
All tasks and job responsibilities must be performed safely without injury to self or others in compliance with System and University safety requirements

How to Apply
Qualified applicants should submit a (1) cover letter, (2) a statement of teaching and research philosophies, (3) detailed vita stating education, experience, and qualifications, (4) copies of transcripts from all colleges attended, and (5) three professional references including names, e-mail addresses, and telephone numbers.
Submit applications here
Address referrals and questions regarding the position to Dr. Jennifer Smith (Jennifer.Smith@tamuk.edu)

Application Deadline: 6 November, 2026 or until a qualified candidate is identified. Preferred start date is June 2027, but start date is negotiable
Contact
Dr. Jennifer Smith
jennifer.smith@tamuk.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
Northern Prairie Wildlife Research Center is seeking 6 -12 student contractor technicians for the 2027 summer field season for Piping Plover studies. Technicians will be placed on crews of 2-3 people and will be responsible for monitoring breeding plovers on emergent sandbars within riverine habitats along the Missouri River in the Northern Great Plains.  They will contribute to nest searching, nest monitoring, erecting predator exclosures, banding adult and chicks, resighting bands with spotting scopes, binoculars, and digital cameras and data entry in Microsoft Access/Survey123.  Students will be trained in data-collection methods at the beginning of the field season. Students will receive motorboat training.
 Field work is extensive and requires long hours walking on river sandbars and operating motorboats in adverse weather conditions. The incumbent may be required to lift containers weighing up to 40 pounds in the performance of assigned duties. Field work will involve exposure to a wide range of weather conditions including cold, mud, and severe heat.  Exposure to biting insects and ticks is possible. At the end of each field day, students are expected to enter data into databases in an office setting. Housing will be provided and may be bunkhouse setting, a field house, camper, and/or apartments.
  This position is only open to students or recent graduates (graduated less than 1 year from start date) (Ex. If graduated in May 2026, you qualify with our April 19th, 2027, start date) Interested applicants should submit their resume, recent copy of transcript, and copy of diploma if applicable. Selections may be made as resumes come in.  
 Start Date: April 19, 2027  may be flexible
 Locations:
Washburn, ND
Bismarck, ND
Yankton, SD   
 Salary: $21.01.-$26.03 depending on position hired for (technician vs crew leader) + free housing 40-60hr/week
 Qualifications: Selectees will be hired as Student Service Contracts.  This position is only open to students or recent graduates (graduated less than 1 year ago from start date) this includes graduate degrees.  Students must be in good academic standing and enrolled in a degree program at a recognized educational institution or be able to show proof of graduation from a recognized educational institution (diploma).
 Must be able to follow an established monitoring protocol and accurately record data.  Students may be required to take and pass the government boat operators course (MOCC) at the beginning of the field season. Description
 *Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A fellowship opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Agricultural Research Service (ARS). This opportunity is remote.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: ARS is updating our strategic planning processes for managing our agricultural research portfolio.  National Program Leaders are collaborating with the Office of Scientific Quality and Review to implement the Agile National Program Cycle (ANPC) and Agricultural Innovation Platform Team processes which are intended to streamline the peer-review process, increase research agility, innovation and relevance, and facilitate the Agency's response to rapidly emerging challenges.  As projects from each of the four divisions of the Office of National Programs (ONP) enter the ANPC, ONP must analyze our progress by collecting, organizing, and maintaining program data using internal ARS systems; prepare data summaries, dashboards, and reports; and support data quality assurance and documentation. 

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Gain experience learning about USDA-ARS strategic planning and agricultural research portfolio management.
Learn how the Agile National Program Cycle and Agricultural Innovation Platform Team processes streamline peer review, improve research agility, and address emerging agricultural challenges.
Learn to collect, organize, maintain, and analyze program data from internal ARS information systems across the Office of National Programs’ four divisions.
Develop skills in data quality assurance, documentation, and standardized management of research-program information.
Collaborate with the mentor to help prepare data summaries, dashboards, and reports to monitor implementation progress.
Build an understanding of how research priorities, peer review, innovation, and portfolio management are integrated within a federal agricultural research agency.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Caird Rexroad (caird.rexroadiii@usda.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: October/November 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for 11-12 months.

Level of Participation: The appointment is part time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.ARS.HQPostdoc@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a bachelor's, master's, or doctoral degree in the one of the relevant fields. 

Preferred skills:

Familiarity with USDA ARS and accompanying data management programs, processes, and community of support for sourcing data to be used in the fellowship.
Proficient with Microsoft Windows, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Adobe.

GENERAL DESCRIPTION:
Under the direction of the Regional Director and working directly with the Wildlife Division Fire Management Coordinator, this position performs advanced (senior-level) consultative services and technical assistance work. Responsible for the oversight and coordination of fire management activities within Region IV and V for the Wildlife Division. Assists TPWD and partner agencies with fire operations statewide.  In coordination with field and program managers, this position implements the Wildlife Division Fire Management Policy and procedures.  Coordinates with local, state and interagency fire management organizations and ensures fire management activities and training programs in the Wildlife Division meet national and state regulatory and accountability standards. Assists field staff with prescribed fire planning, preparation and implementation activities on state-owned/managed and private lands.  Creates, compiles and disseminates fire related incident reports and records. Maintains fire program safety in a high-risk environment, including public and staff safety as well as infrastructure protection.  Manages fire equipment and fire cache supplies.  Assists with specifications, maintenance and preparedness of equipment and staff resources.  Works with managers and project leaders to mentor, evaluate and certify Division staff and track staff qualifications and certifications in the Incident Qualifications System database.  Promotes and assists project leaders, district leaders and field staff in establishing and achieving fire management goals and developing training and experience opportunities to advance staff qualifications.  Serves on the TPWD Incident Management Team as needed for All Hazard Emergency Response and large planned fire events.  Conducts public outreach events on fire management. Works under limited supervision, with considerable latitude for the use of initiative and independent judgment. Performs additional duties as assigned. Complies with all Agency, Division and Branch rules, regulations and procedures.

MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS:

Education: 
Graduation from an accredited college or university with a Bachelor's degree in Natural Resources Management, Agriculture, Wildlife Management, Rangeland Management, Fire Ecology or closely related field.

Experience:
Five years of experience in Natural Resources Management, Conservation Science, Fire Management, Fire Ecology or closely related field. 

Five years of experience in wildland fire management to include writing, reviewing, and critiquing prescribed burn unit plans and area fire management plans.

NOTE: Experience may have occurred concurrently.

Licensure:        
Must possess or be able to obtain, within 30 days of employment, a valid state driver's license.
Must possess current National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) FFT1 Trainee certification.  (Must provide copy of current NWCG qualifications and IQCS master record or equivalent with job application and resume).
Must possess the National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) Single Resource Boss and Firing Boss certification.
Must possess the National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) Type IV Incident Commander certification. 
Must possess the National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) Type II Burn Boss (RXB2) certification.
Must possess or be able to obtain, within one year of employment, certification as a TPWD Burn Boss according to Texas Prescribed Burn Board standards for prescribed Burn Manager.
NOTE: Retention of position contingent upon obtaining and maintaining required licenses and certifications.

Physical Requirements:

Must be able to pass, within one year of employment, the FFTII arduous duty physical fitness standard (walk 3 miles with 45 lb. pack in 45 minutes or less).   

NOTE: Retention of position contingent upon meeting and maintaining physical requirements.

ACCEPTABLE SUBSTITUTIONS:
Education: 
Ten years of experience in Wildland Fire Management to include writing, reviewing, and critiquing prescribed burn unit plans and area fire management plans, may substitute for the required education.

Five years of experience as a National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) Type II Burn Boss (RXB2), may substitute for the required education.

Experience:
Graduation from an accredited college or university with a Master's degree in Natural Resources Management, Agriculture, Wildlife Management, Rangeland Management, Fire Ecology or closely related field, may substitute for one year of required experience in Natural Resources Management, Conservation Science, Fire Management, Fire Ecology or closely related field. 

Graduation from an accredited college or university with a PhD in Natural Resources Management, Agriculture, Wildlife Management, Rangeland Management, Fire Ecology or closely related field, may substitute for two years of required experience in Natural Resources Management, Conservation Science, Fire Management, Fire Ecology or closely related field.

Experience: 
Experience developing land management objectives.
Experience in implementing fire management activities in Texas fuel models and vegetation types.
Experience in resource and habitat management.
Experience with GPS data collection and processing and using GIS applications.
Experience using or prescribing land management tools such as prescribed fire, selective thinning, grazing etc.

Experience with sound, science-based decision making as it relates to fire and natural resources management.
Experience in NWCG training and curriculum design.

Knowledge of NWCG standards, guidelines and training requirements.
Knowledge of community based natural resource management and research techniques and methodologies.
Knowledge of technical report writing and photographic skills.
Knowledge of microcomputer systems and use of computerized databases.
Knowledge of wildland fire behavior and fire management planning.
Knowledge of current trends and practices in fire management, land management, grazing management, and natural resource conservation.

    Description
 The Avian Ecology Program at Archbold Biological Station is seeking four Post-Baccalaureate Research Fellows (PBRFs) for seasonal appointments of at least six months to assist with one of the world's longest-running studies of wild birds: a 57-year research program focused on the demography, ecology, behavior, and conservation of the federally threatened Florida Scrub-Jay (Aphelocoma coerulescens). Four positions will begin on February 1, 2027. Two appointments will continue through July 2027, while the remaining two will continue through mid-September 2027. 

 Fellows will be mentored by Dr. Sahas Barve and work within a dynamic research team that includes three research assistants. This is a seasonal position paying $15.00 per hour for approximately 29 hours per week. Because this position is classified as seasonal, traditional employee benefits are not provided at hire. Archbold determines benefit eligibility for seasonal employees using the Affordable Care Act (ACA) look-back measurement method. 

 Lodging is provided, and residence at Archbold Biological Station is required for the duration of the fellowship. 

 A unique feature of this fellowship is the opportunity to develop an independent research project, either through the collection of new field data or by leveraging Archbold's extensive long-term Florida Scrub-Jay dataset. We particularly encourage applications from individuals who are enthusiastic about pursuing independent research and gaining hands-on experience in ecological field studies, data analysis, and scientific inquiry. 

 
Requirements
Key Responsibilities 
 PBRFs contribute to several aspects of this research, but their primary duties include:  
 Independently searching for and monitoring nests  
 Conducting monthly censuses of color-banded birds 
 Daily data entry 
 Habituating birds for subsequent trapping 
 Conducting oak acorn surveys  
 Surveying FLSJ populations at other sites 
 In addition, PBRFs may assist in collecting blood samples from jays, mapping jay territories, and helping with prescribed fires  

Required Qualifications 
 Bachelor’s degree. This position is ideal for students with undergraduate degrees contemplating graduate school in the fields of Ecology, Evolution, Conservation Biology, and Natural Resource Management.  


 Experience
 Field experience outside of coursework; however, we provide all required training for all PBRFs.  
 Resighting color-banded birds 
 Finding and monitoring nests 
 Using a compass or GPS  
 Ability to navigate and work alone in the field but coordinate duties with a small team to achieve all project goals. 
 Certifications/Licenses 
 A valid US Driver’s License  
 Experience searching for nests of open-cup nesters, preferred 
 Please note that we are unable to provide international applicants with a work visa. US citizenship or permission to work legally in the US is required.


 Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities
 Attention to detail with respect to following sampling protocols and managing data 
 Tolerance for biting insects, early mornings, and high heat/humidity 
 Motivation and enthusiasm about living and working at a rural field-station 
 Respect for others, as PBRFs will share lodging with other PBRFs 
 Effective and responsive communication with supervisors, coworkers, and roommates 

 
Work Environment & Physical Requirements
 Employees must be able to perform the essential functions of their position with or without reasonable accommodation. Depending on the role, work may require sitting, standing, walking, bending, reaching, lifting and carrying materials, repetitive hand movements, and operating standard office, laboratory, field, or maintenance equipment. Some positions may involve working outdoors in varying weather conditions, traversing uneven terrain, and occasional travel. Physical requirements will vary by position and will be specified in the individual job description. 
   

 Why Join Archbold?
 Joining Archbold means becoming part of a mission-driven organization dedicated to advancing scientific research, conservation, and education. Employees have the opportunity to contribute meaningful work that supports the understanding and preservation of natural ecosystems while collaborating with passionate, talented professionals. Archbold fosters a culture of innovation, teamwork, and continuous learning, providing an environment where employees can grow professionally while making a lasting impact on science, conservation, and the communities we serve. Eligible employees also enjoy competitive compensation and benefits package designed to support their well-being and professional success. 

    How to Apply
 Complete the application here, and include the following in a single pdf titled with your surname: 
 A single-page cover letter outlining how your previous experiences and interests are relevant to the job responsibilities and qualifications listed above. Be sure to mention your research interests and describe how this position aligns with your personal experiences and goals. 
A CV
The names and contact information of three references 


For questions, please contact Hannah Miller (avianecol@archbold-station.org). We will start reviewing applications after the deadline on October 20, 2026, and hope to finalize hires by ~1 month after this date.
