Description
 *Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis and applications may close before the deadline.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS).

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

The USDA ARS Beneficial Insects Introduction Research Unit, located on the University of Delaware campus in Newark, Delaware, maintains a certified quarantine facility that enables pioneering research on the biological control of invasive agricultural and forest insect pests.

Research Project: Under guidance of the mentor, you will assist in determining the host associations of introduced biological control agents with the invasive emerald ash borer (EAB) and other related pests. Part of this research will be quantifying the impacts of these introduced agents on pest population densities in long-term EAB biological control study sites. Research activities will occur both in a laboratory quarantine facility and in agricultural fields or forests across the United States.

Learning Objectives: During the appointment, you will;

Gain hands-on experience rearing and maintaining colonies of emerald ash borer (EAB) and its larval and egg parasitoids.
Learn to conduct field and laboratory experiments to assess host associations between field-collected parasitoids, emerald ash borer, and related Agrilus beetle species.
Develop skills in entering, curating, organizing, and managing experimental data generated from EAB and parasitoid studies.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Jian Duan (jian.duan@usda.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: October 30, 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for nine months, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.ARS.Northeast@orau.org  and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a bachelor's or master's degree in the one of the relevant fields. Degree must have been received within the past five years, or anticipated to be received by 1/31/2027.

Preferred skills:

Candidates with experiences in rearing insects and biological control research are preferred

Description
As a Fisheries Biologist II, you’ll play a key role in the research and management of invasive carp within the Ohio River and its tributaries. This position is responsible for planning and conducting various fisheries assessments, analyzing biological data, and developing management recommendations related to invasive carp and ANS management. The successful candidate will have experience and knowledge with database programs, fish and wildlife programs and projects, strong organizational skills, and a strong work ethic. Required work hours are 37.5 hours per week; however, overtime and irregular shifts may be required for the completion of projects.
 
 In this role, you will:
Conduct electrofishing and other fish population surveys on rivers
Analyze biological data and prepare technical reports
Develop and implement management plans and recommendations
Provide input on regulation changes and fisheries policy
Coordinate with partners, stakeholders, and the public

This is a grant funded time-limited (GFTL) position. This means it is a position that is paid entirely as the result of a grant. The duration of employment shall not exceed the life of the grant that funds the position. An employee appointed to a GFTL position is required to meet the minimum requirements for the classification. Further, an employee appointed to a GFTL position is designated as an unclassified (non-merit) employee. A GFTL employee is eligible to receive benefits at the same level as a classified (merit) employee in a permanent position.
 
 Work is field-oriented and hands-on, often performed outdoors in varying weather conditions and river environments. This position requires strong organizational skills, biological knowledge, and the ability to work both independently and as part of a team. The Fisheries Biologist II classification includes responsibility for project leadership, data analysis, reporting, and contributing to statewide fisheries management objectives. 

If you’re passionate about rivers, fish populations, and science-based resource management, this is your opportunity to make a meaningful impact on Kentucky’s aquatic resources. The position has opportunities for advancement into senior biologist role as experience and performance warrant.
 
 Join us in conserving and enhancing Kentucky’s rivers for current and future generations of anglers and outdoor enthusiasts.
 
 Preferred Skills: Proficient with boat trailering and operation in various waterbodies and weather conditions. Well versed in freshwater fish identification, and conducting fish sampling techniques including gill nets, electrofishing, and trawls. Must be able to swim. Proficient with Microsoft programs including Word, Excel, and Power Point and data analysis with SAS or program R preferred. 

Minimum Requirements
EDUCATION: Graduate of a college or university with a bachelor's degree. Transcript review must indicate that the following course work has been earned at the undergraduate or graduate level: 1. Biological Sciences: 30 semester hours (45 quarter hours) in biological sciences. Four courses (12 semester or 18 quarter hours) must be in Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences; 6 of the 12 required semester hours must be directly related to fisheries science and at least one course (3 semester hours) must cover the principles of fisheries science and management. These courses may include fish management, ichthyology, aquaculture, fish ecology, principles of fisheries science, limnology, and stream ecology. The remaining hours can include other biological science courses such as biology, botany, and ecology. Examples of courses include biology, botany, ecology, cellular biology, fish management, ichthyology and limnology. 2. Physical Sciences: 15 semester hours (23 quarter hours) in physical sciences. Examples of courses are chemistry, physics, hydrology, astronomy, earth science and meteorology. 3. Mathematics and Statistics: 6 semester hours (9 quarter hours) in mathematics and statistics. Must include one calculus and one statistics OR two statistics courses. 4. Communications and Human Dimensions: 9 semester hours (13quarter hours) in communications and human dimensions. Courses include verbal and writing courses that include public speaking, discussion, composition and technical writing. Up to 3 semester hours related to Master's thesis or PhD dissertation course work will count towards the 9 semester hour requirement. Human dimensions can include courses in areas of human personnel management, conflict resolution, socioeconomic and survey techniques.
 EXPERIENCE, TRAINING, OR SKILLS: Must have one years of professional experience in fishery research, fishery management and, or, a related field.
 Substitute EDUCATION for EXPERIENCE: Certification by The American Fisheries Society at the Associate Fisheries Professional or Certified Fisheries Professional level will substitute for the education requirements. For additional information on The American Fisheries Society refer to https://fisheries.org/ A master's degree in fishery management, fishery biology or a related field will substitute for one year of the required experience.
 Substitute EXPERIENCE for EDUCATION: NONE
 SPECIAL REQUIREMENTS (AGE, LICENSURE, REGULATION, ETC.): Must possess a valid driver's license prior to appointment in this classification. Must maintain any required licensure(s), certification(s), or other credentials for the length of employment in this classification. Employing agency is responsible for ensuring employee possesses and maintains required licensure(s), certification(s) or other credentials.
Contact
jeffrey herod
jeffrey.herod@ky.gov (preferred contact method)

Description
The New Mexico Highlands University Department of Forestry invites applicants to fill one or more nine-month, tenure-track faculty positions beginning as early as August 2027.

The successful candidates will be responsible for teaching a range of forestry and natural resources management courses per academic year; conducting research and scholarship that engages both undergraduate and graduate students; serving the University, professional organizations, and the broader community of natural resources stakeholders; advising Forestry Department students; contributing to the modernization and improvement of the Forestry and Conservation Management curricula; participating in the Forestry Department’s outcomes assessments, aiding in the maintenance of Society of American Foresters (SAF) accreditation, and establishing and maintaining relationships with industry, tribal, governmental, and non-governmental partners. Preferred areas of specialization include tree ecophysiology, forest ecohydrology, water resources or watershed management.  Regardless of specialty, individuals with proficiency in plant production and forest nursery management, applied forest ecology, and forest management and GIS are strongly encouraged to apply. 

This position is part of the NMHU College of Arts and Sciences’ initiative to strengthen its Forestry Department’s teaching and research capabilities. The College of Arts and Sciences, housed within a Hispanic Serving Institution, is dedicated to creating a climate of engagement, diversity and inclusion, and providing pathways for students from underrepresented groups to pursue STEM careers. All applicants should have a demonstrated willingness to work collaboratively with faculty from a wide range of disciplines, cultures, and academic backgrounds and to advise and teach an undergraduate and graduate student body that is diverse with respect to socio-economic status, culture, and career path.

The successful candidate will be expected to seek and acquire external research support and collaborate with universities, state and federal government agencies, and non-governmental organizations in the areas of specialization. 

The New Mexico Forest and Watershed Restoration Institute, which is housed on NMHU’s main campus, utilizes NMHU faculty members and students in projects throughout the state. NMHU Forestry faculty also regularly collaborate with the faculty and staff of New Mexico State University's (NMSU) John T. Harrington Forestry Research Center in Mora, NM, as well as the New Mexico Reforestation Center, with facilities and operations in both Mora, NM and on NMHU’s Las Vegas campus. Building upon our current strengths, the incumbent will be expected to contribute to the development of a nationally recognized education, research, and outreach program focused on forest or wildland fire management and/or forest or wildland ecosystem health. Preference will be given to candidates with a demonstrated ability or willingness to concentrate on these themes in relation to Southern Rocky Mountains and Southwestern ecosystems. USDA Forest Service Office/Lab and Location: A fellowship opportunity is available with the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Forest Service (FS) within the Pacific Northwest Research Station (PNWRS) located in Arcata, California.

At the heart of the USDA Forest Service's mission is their purpose. Everything they do is intended to help sustain forests and grasslands for present and future generations. Why? Because their stewardship work supports nature in sustaining life. This is the purpose that drives the agency’s mission and motivates their work across the agency. It’s been there from the agency’s very beginning, and it still drives them. To advance the mission and serve their purpose, the USDA Forest Service balances the short and long-term needs of people and nature by: working in collaboration with communities and our partners; providing access to resources and experiences that promote economic, ecological, and social vitality; connecting people to the land and one another; and delivering world-class science, technology and land management.

Research Project: This project evaluates potential modifications of infrastructure aimed at reducing bat fatalities at energy facilities.  Two species of bats will be evaluated.  Both species are forest-obligate species found on all National Forests.  They are also the 2 species most frequently killed via energy infrastructure.  The research involves observational studies of bats interactions with infrastructure as well as capture of individuals that are observed in choice experiments conducted in the field. Results will be shared through publications and presentations to energy developers and forest managers considering energy infrastructure installations on their lands.  

We have an opportunity for a fellow to be a part of this learning experience in the construction of experimental apparatus in the field, capture and handle bats, conduct choice experiments with captured bats, deploy and monitor audio and video recordings, process resulting data streams, and analyze these data.   The opportunity includes opportunities to participate in the development and presentation of results in reports, publications, workshops, and conferences.   This will be conducted in Humboldt County, California and includes opportunities to interact with a wide range of collaborators including academics, government employees, community members, university students, and energy industry representatives.  

Learning Objectives: 

Detail how energy infrastructure can affect bat behavior and contribute to bat fatalities.
Develop an understanding of the ecology and conservation needs of two forest-obligate bat species commonly affected by energy facilities.
Preform safe, ethical techniques for capturing, handling, and releasing bats during field-based choice experiments.
Conduct behavioral observations and controlled choice experiments with bats in natural settings.
Communicate scientific results through reports, publications, workshops, conference presentations, and outreach to energy developers and forest managers.
Mentor: The mentor for this opportunity is Theodore Weller (theodore.weller@usda.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for 8 months but may be extended upon recommendation of USDA Forest Service and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Participants do not become employees of USDA, USDA Forest Service, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

The qualified candidate should have received a bachelor's or master's degree in the one of the relevant fields. Degree must have been received within the past five years.

Experience capturing bats or birds in mist nets. 
Experience managing large volumes of field data. 
Experience analyzing audio or video recordings of wildlife, especially bats.

Description

EPA Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention (OCSPP), Great Lakes Coastal Environmental Science Laboratory located in Duluth, Minnesota.

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; National efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; Federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: The US EPA is mandated to address the endocrine disrupting potential of thousands of chemicals. For the majority of these chemicals there is a lack of information regarding whether they have the potential to cause adverse effects from impacts on thyroid hormone status. Understanding the important targets within the network of processes involved in maintaining normal functioning thyroid hormone levels, and what approaches to best assess activity at those targets are critical to developing a comprehensive approach to evaluating thyroid hormone disrupting potential of large numbers of chemicals.  

Recently, a number of thyroid-related in vitro high-throughput screening (HTS) assays have been developed to broaden assay coverage for molecular targets potentially leading to thyroid disruption and were implemented to screen US EPA’s ToxCast Phase 1, 2 and E1K chemical libraries. This battery of thyroid-related in vitro HTS assays can be employed to rapidly assess potential interference with these targets. However, this screening approach leaves uncertainties regarding the meaning of in vitro activity data as it relates to in vivo adverse outcomes. Part of this research effort aims to develop a translational process that integrates relevant information, models, and data streams to provide richer context to interpret in vitro results related to thyroid disruption. As part of the translational process, this research opportunity will focus on the development of a bio-assay to quantitative monitor thyroid hormone synthesis as a complimentary assay to existing in vitro thyroid-related assays. Assay development will be followed by the analysis of canonical and suspected thyroid disrupting chemicals to understand whether, or how, in vitro activity of chemicals translates to in vivo outcomes. Additionally, this research will employ existing computational tools such as the octanol-water partition coefficient (logKow) and quantitative structure-activity relationships (QSAR) models to provide deeper interpretation of in vitro data and further prioritize chemicals most likely to impact thyroid function in aquatic systems. The translational principles employed will have much broader applicability across ToxCast HTS assays and aquatic vertebrates. 

With guidance from the mentor, you may be involved in any or all of the following training activities:

Analyzing gene expression using real-time polymerase chain reaction and developing novel primers, probes, and standards for gene expression analyses.
Developing high-throughput techniques for collection, batch processing, and analysis of biofluid and tissue samples suitable for molecular, biochemical, and/or histological analyses.
Conducting aquatic toxicology experiment using flow-through exposure systems. 
Developing and evaluating exposure strategies suitable for methodologically-challenging chemicals such as highly non-polar substances (e.g., high octanol-water partitioning coefficients), volatile chemicals, reactive chemicals, etc.
Performing quality assurance and quality control of experimental data and processes. 
Processing and analyzing large, high content, data sets using both existing and novel computational pipelines.
Analyzing experimental data and generating tables, figures, and other summaries of results.
Conducting statistical analyses including the use of hypothesis testing, regression-based approaches, multi-variate statistics, concordance analyses, etc.
Presenting research results at scientific meetings and participating in written reports and journal articles.
Learning Objectives:  You will join and learn from a transdisciplinary research team engaged in multiple aspects of project planning, communication, research implementation, and analysis. You will have the opportunity to interact with internationally recognized leaders, both within and outside EPA. 

During this appointment, you will:

Learn how to participate in and/or publish original research.
Learn a breadth of laboratory, analytical, and computational techniques which can be applied across life sciences research fields.
Learn to operate and use a range of scientific equipment.
Learn to evaluate data quality, trouble shoot research results, apply statistical methods for data analysis and interpretation.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Sigmund Degitz (Degitz.Sigmund@epa.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research please contact the mentor.

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: September 2026. All start dates are flexible and vary depending on numerous factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, and may be renewed three to four additional years upon EPA recommendation and subject to availability of funding.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Participant Stipend: The participant will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens and Lawful Permanent Residents (LPR) only.

EPA Security Clearance: Completion of a successful background investigation by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is required for an applicant to be on-boarded at EPA.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and EPA. Participants do not become employees of EPA, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

ORISE offers all ORISE EPA graduate students and Postdocs a free 5 year membership to the National Postdoctoral Association (NPA).

The successful applicant(s) will be required to comply with Environmental, Safety and Health (ES&H) requirements of the hosting facility.

Questions: Please see the FAQ section of our website. If you have additional questions about the application process please email ORISE.EPA.Other@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should have received a master's or bachelor's degree in one of the relevant fields (Toxicology, Biochemistry, Biology or related sub-disciplines like molecular biology, fisheries biology, computational biology). Candidates with a bachelor's degree may be considered if they can demonstrate strong laboratory experience. Degree must have been received within the past 5 years.

Preferred Skills:

Experience conducting bioassays at the in vitro and in vivo.
Previous experience with aquatic organisms such as fish and amphibians.
Experience with basic molecular biology techniques used for analysis of proteins and nucleic acids (e.g., gel electrophoresis, PCR, quantitative real-time PCR, use of thermocyclers and/or bioanalyzers, DNA sequencer etc.)
Previous research experience, beyond lab-oriented coursework alone.
Previous experience writing peer reviewed journal articles.
Previous experience with science communication to a diversity of technical and non-technical audiences.
Computational skills (e.g., programming, R-based statistics)
Previous experience engaging with omics data and/or high throughput data sets such as those from EPA's ToxCast program.

Description
 We are seeking a highly motivated Postdoctoral Associate to join the laboratory of Samantha M. Wisely for a research project investigating the landscape genetics and molecular ecology of Wild Turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo) in Florida. 

The successful candidate will lead genetic and genomic analyses designed to better understand the ecological and evolutionary processes influencing Wild Turkey populations across Florida. The project will integrate molecular data with spatial and ecological information to investigate patterns of genetic connectivity, population structure, dispersal, relatedness, and reproduction across heterogeneous landscapes. 

A major emphasis of the position will be the use of spatial and landscape genetic approaches to determine how environmental and anthropogenic landscape features influence gene flow and population connectivity. The project will also incorporate parentage and relatedness analyses to examine reproductive relationships and fine-scale patterns of movement and population structure. 


Primary Responsibilities 

The successful candidate will be expected to: 

·         Lead analyses of molecular genetic/genomic datasets from Wild Turkey populations throughout Florida. 

·         Conduct population genetic and landscape genetic analyses, including assessment of population structure, genetic differentiation, connectivity, and gene flow. 

·         Integrate genetic data with GIS and spatial environmental datasets to evaluate landscape effects on genetic connectivity and dispersal. 

·         Conduct parentage, kinship, and relatedness analyses to investigate reproductive relationships and fine-scale population processes. 

·         Collaborate with project investigators, graduate students, agency biologists, and other research partners. 

·         Prepare manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed journals and present findings at professional scientific meetings. 

·         Assist with mentoring graduate and undergraduate students involved in molecular ecology and wildlife research. 

·         Contribute intellectually to the development of additional research questions and proposals emerging from the project. 


Required Qualifications 

Applicants must have: 

·         A Ph.D. in molecular ecology, conservation genetics, landscape genetics, population genetics, wildlife genomics, or a closely related field by the anticipated start date. 

·         Demonstrated experience analyzing population genetic or genomic datasets. 

·         Experience working in R and/or other programming environments used for genetic and ecological analyses. 

·         A demonstrated ability to conduct independent research and manage large or complex datasets. 

·         Excellent written and oral communication skills. 

·         Ability to work effectively as part of a collaborative, multidisciplinary research team. 


Preferred Qualifications 

Preference will be given to candidates with one or more of the following: 

·         Experience conducting landscape genetic analyses of wildlife populations. 

·         Experience integrating molecular data with GIS, remote-sensing, land-cover, or other spatial datasets. 

·         Expertise with SNP, reduced-representation genomic, or other contemporary molecular datasets. 

·         Experience with population assignment, individual identification, genetic estimates of dispersal, or connectivity modeling. 

·         Experience with parentage analysis involving wild populations. 

·         Familiarity with spatially explicit models of gene flow or resistance/connectivity modeling. 

·         Familiarity with reproducible research workflows, version control, or high-performance computing. 


Research Environment 

The successful applicant will join the Wisely Lab at the University of Florida, an interdisciplinary research group working at the interface of wildlife ecology, molecular ecology, conservation genetics, disease ecology, and wildlife management. 


Expected Salary and Commitment 

Salary will be commensurate with qualifications and experience and consistent with University of Florida guidelines for Postdoctoral Associates. This is a term position for one year with the possibility for renewal for a second year. 


Special Instructions to Applicants 

Please submit the following to wiselylab@ifas.ufl.edu 

1.      Cover letter describing research interests, relevant experience, and qualifications for the position. The cover letter should specifically describe the applicant's experience with population or landscape genetics, spatial analysis, and parentage/relatedness analysis. 

2.      Curriculum vitae. 

3.      Contact information for three professional references. 

4.      One representative peer-reviewed publication that best demonstrates the applicant's relevant research experience. 

Review of applications will begin November 15th  and will continue until the position is filled. 

Contact
Samantha M Wisely
3528460645
wisely@ufl.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
Title- Ballast Water Vessel Inspector
Classification- Marine Transportation and Safety Specialist 3
Job Status- Full-Time / Permanent
WDFW Program- Fish Program – Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) Management
Duty Station- Ridgefield, Washington – Clark County

Learn more about being a member of Team WDFW!


As the Ballast Water Vessel Inspector, you’ll help protect Washington’s waters from aquatic invasive species and support the long-term health of our marine ecosystems.

In this role, you’ll train to conduct onboard inspections of commercial vessels arriving in Washington State to ensure compliance with ballast water management regulations designed to prevent the spread of invasive species. You’ll work in active port environments throughout the Columbia River, Greys Harbor, and South Puget Sound.

This is a great opportunity for someone interested in maritime operations, environmental compliance, vessel inspection, and protecting Washington’s natural resources through hands-on fieldwork and regulatory enforcement.


What to Expect:
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Ballast Water Vessel Inspector will,

Vessel Ballast Water Risk Audits:
Assess daily vessel arrivals to identify the highest ballast water risks using vessel compliance history, department protocols, and professional judgement.
Select, board, and inspect at least 5% of all targeted vessel arrivals in assigned region.
Explain state laws and regulations and assist vessel officers and crew in meeting compliance objectives for state ballast water management.
Complete required department inspection forms per protocols.

Compliance Actions:
Assess onboard evidence of ballast water management compliance using vessel records, equipment specifications, and certifications.
Investigate and issue appropriate compliance actions per department protocols for vessel situations including Warnings, Notices of Correction, or recommendations for Notice of Penalty.
Compile evidence to create professional and legally defensible compliance actions.

Coordination, Planning, and Reporting:
Coordinate with the U.S. Coast Guard, Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, and Washington Department of Ecology to support cooperative vessel management and minimize duplication of efforts on concurrent vessel boardings.
Analyze, evaluate, and interpret vessel inspection data.
Support the development and implementation of work plans, regulatory updates, performance measures, management forms, protocols, and procedures. 
Participate in state, regional, and national work groups as assigned.

Monitoring and Research:
Conduct onboard testing of new protocols and equipment as directed.
Analyze ballast water treatment system (BWTS) voyage maintenance records and annual independent laboratory performance test reports to support the development of new regulatory requirements.
Assist senior staff in developing and evaluating enhanced vessel ballast water and biofouling risk assessment protocols.
Develop, evaluate, and interpret protocols, tools, and performance measures used to assess the effectiveness of ballast water management practices.
 

Working Conditions: 

Work Setting, including hazards:
Work is performed in potentially hazardous industrial port environments aboard merchant vessels conducting cargo operations. Board and inspect all types of vessels in a variety of weather conditions and physically access all areas of vessels, including climbing ladders and entering engine/pump rooms, and occasionally, ballast tanks to inspect ballast management activities. Frequently lift and carry a 40-pound gear bag. Handle hazardous biological sample preservation chemicals, such as Formalin and ethanol. This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.

Schedule:
This position is full-time, working 40 hours per week. The standard work schedule includes the potential for occasional evening or weekend work as needed. Schedules may vary based on business needs, time of year, and/or weather conditions.

Travel Requirements:
Travel between state ports is required and may average approximately 1,500 to 3,000 miles per month.

Tools and Equipment:
Use appropriate safety equipment including flotation devices, hard hats, safety goggles, and steel-toed boots. 

Customer Interactions:
Regular interaction with regulated industry representatives, including situations that may be complex or confrontational. Communication may also involve working with individuals for whom English is a secondary language.
 

Qualifications:

Required Qualifications:

Option 1– All of the following:
A Bachelor of Science or Master's degree involving major study in one of the following:  
Marine Engineering
Nautical Industrial Science
Naval Architecture
A closely related field
*Four (4) years of professional-level experience in vessel design or vessel inspection.

Option 2 – All of the following (experience may be gained concurrently):
A Bachelor of Science or Master’s degree involving major study in one of the following: 
Environmental Planning 
Natural Sciences 
A closely related field
*Four (4) years of professional-level experience in maritime operations, aquatic invasive species management, environmental compliance, or closely related regulatory or scientific work. 
Including at least two (2) years of professional-level experience in vessel design or vessel inspection.

Option 3– All of the following:
A PhD in one of the following: 
Environmental Planning
Marine Engineering
Natural Sciences
Nautical Industrial Science
Naval Architecture 
A closely related field
*Two (2) years of professional-level experience in vessel design or vessel inspection.

*Qualifying experience must include substantial professional-level work in at least two (2) of the knowledge areas listed below, including at least one (1) area from Part A and one (1) area from Part B:

Part A:
Shipping regulatory and management operations.
Vessel operations.
Vessel and port safety requirements.
Vessel ballast water management system operations, testing, and quality control requirements used for regulatory purposes.
Other related commercial vessel inspection duties, such as oil spill prevention and other vessel discharge.

Part B:
Marine and freshwater Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) risks to the state, including ballast water and biofouling pathways and management techniques. 
Working effectively with diverse vessel managers, agents, officers, and crew.
Field research, sampling, monitoring, and testing techniques.
Other related natural resource duties and responsibilities, such as fishery observations and environmental compliance.

Please Note:
Closely related qualifying experience may be substituted for the required education on a year-by-year basis.
A current Maritime License for Marine Officer or Marine Engineer may substitute for the education requirement.

Certifications/Licenses:
Valid driver’s license.

Special Requirements/Conditions of Employment:
This position will be required to undergo a federal background check as part of obtaining a Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC) or similar federal credential.


Preferred Qualifications:
In addition to the required qualifications, our ideal applicant will possess one or more of the following:
Results Orientation and Initiative: Focuses on results and desired outcomes and how best to achieve them. Proactively identifies needs and takes appropriate action.
Decision Making: Ability to make independent decisions in a manner that produces outcomes that are consistent with Agency, Program, and Division policy is essential. Appropriately involves supervisor or others in decision making.
Communication: Demonstrates clear, concise written and verbal communication skills. Keeps supervisors and co-workers informed of need to know items.
Planning: Uses strategic thinking to evaluate proposed actions and timelines against organizational mission and values. Integrates current plans with other plans as needed to achieve the overall mission.
Relationship Building and Collaboration: Develop and maintain effective internal and external partnerships that promote and support the Agency’s mission and goals.
 

Your application should include the following:
A completed online application showcasing how your qualifications align with the job requirements.
An up-to-date resume.
A cover letter detailing your interest in the position, your relevant skills and experience, and why you are the ideal candidate.
At least three (3) professional references with current contact information.

Description

The U.S.D.A. Forest Service Pacific Northwest Research Station and the Wallowa-Whitman and Umatilla National Forests have been monitoring avian and mammalian wildlife in these forests to quantify wildlife responses to forest management actions to ultimately inform management decision making. The primary focus of the work is deploying passive monitoring devices, including audio recording units and game cameras. However, the work will also include more traditional wildlife fieldwork like conducting nest searches and nest checks for white-headed woodpecker and tracking white-headed woodpecker using VHF transmitters. Start date is flexible, this position will initially be focused on office duties, training, and data validation before the field season begins in late March.

Position Announcements:

·         Forestry Technician (Recreation, Timber, Range), GS-5: https://www.usajobs.gov/job/886147500 
·         Forestry Technician (Recreation, Timber, Range), GS-6: https://www.usajobs.gov/job/886148000 
·         Forestry Technician (Recreation, Timber, Range), GS-7: https://www.usajobs.gov/job/886148100 
·         Please note: the positions are titled Forestry Technician (Recreation, Timber, Range), please use application materials to reflect requirements in the 
USAJobs posting.

Duties include:

·         Validate acoustic avian detections
·         Deploy/retrieve audio recording units and game cameras 
·         Conduct white-headed woodpecker nest searches and nest checks
·         Track white-headed woodpeckers using VHF transmitters
·         Collect, record, and verify data
·         GS-7 position will serve as an assistant crew leader and assist with training field crew

Requirements: 

·         U.S. Citizen or U.S. National
·         Valid state driver’s license
·         Must be 18 years of age
·         Must be able to work independently and in groups
·         Must have good observational and communication skills
·         Comfortable working in remote locations in steep forested terrain, often in inclement weather, including snow, rain and heat
·         Previous field experience and experience navigating remote landscapes using a map and GPS is desirable
·         Good to excellent hearing and familiarity with vocalizations of PNW wildlife species and/or experience with radio telemetry in the field is a definite plus, but not a requirement
·         Background check will be required

GS-5 Level

·         One year of specialized experience relating to wildlife or natural resources management programs or 4 years of successfully completed education above high school (120 semester/180 quarter hours) leading to a bachelor’s degree with major study in forestry, range management, agriculture, or a subject-matter field directly related to the position, or that included at least 24 semester hours in any combination of courses directly related to the position such as forestry, agriculture, crop or plant science, range management or conservation, wildlife management, watershed management, soil science, natural resources, outdoor recreation management, civil or forest engineering, or wildland fire science (no more than 6 semester hours in mathematics is creditable). 

OR

·         A combination of experience and education to meet the total experience required. The education must have been obtained in an accredited college or university.

GS-6 Level

·         Four years of successfully completed education above high school (120 semester/180 quarter hours) leading to a bachelor’s degree with major study in wildlife or other related fields, that included at least 24 semester hours in any combination of courses directly related to the position such as forestry, agriculture, crop or plant science, range management or conservation, wildlife management, watershed management, soil science, natural resources, outdoor recreation management, civil or forest engineering, or wildland fire science (no more than 6 semester hours in mathematics is creditable).
·         One year of specialized experience relating to wildlife or natural resources management programs equivalent to the GS-5 level.

GS-7 Level

·         One year of specialized experience relating to wildlife or natural resources management programs equivalent to the GS-6 level.

OR

·         One full year (18 semester/27 quarter hours) of successfully completed graduate level coursework that is directly related to the work of the position (such as forestry, agriculture, crop or plant science, range management or conservation, wildlife management, watershed management, soil science, natural resources, outdoor recreation management, civil or forest engineering, or wildland fire).

OR

·         Combinations of graduate level education that is directly related to the position and specialized experience. The education must have been obtained in an accredited college or university.

 

Benefits:

·         Up to $34,799 per year (GS-5 level)
·         Up to $38,791 per year (GS-6 level)
·         Up to $43,106 per year (GS-7 level)
·         Work vehicle and field equipment provided (not including personal transportation needs)

How to Apply:

These positions will be open for applications on USA Jobs on September 25th, 2026. Positions will be advertised as Forestry Technician (Recreation, Timber, Range). Be sure to select La Grande, OR as a duty station.

Please note, there is a two-page resume page limit for applications.

Description
 *Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), located in Athens, Georgia.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: You will be part of the research team learning about developing recombinant Marek's disease virus vaccines to prevent both Marek's disease and other poultry diseases. The project involves the construction of recombinant vaccines using molecularly cloned Marek's disease virus as a vector platform and the evaluation of the efficacy against Marek's disease and targeted poultry disease. You will construct the recombinant Marek's disease virus that expresses the foreign antigens. You will learn the construction of recombinant avian herpesvirus vaccines, conduct vaccine efficacy studies to develop novel poultry vaccines, including sample collection from animals, execution of viral genome detection, and data analysis.

Learning Objectives: During the fellowship, you will acquire the following skills and knowledge through hands-on training:

Recovery of Infectious Avian Herpesviruses: You will learn the techniques required to recover infectious avian herpesviruses from DNA transfection processes, gaining a deeper understanding of molecular virology and virus recovery methods.

Quantification of Virus Infectivity and Titer: You will be trained to accurately quantify virus infectivity and determine viral titers, developing expertise in virological assays and data interpretation.

Modification of Cloned Virus Genome: You gain proficiency in using advanced recombineering technologies to modify cloned virus genomes, learning how to apply genetic engineering techniques for the study and manipulation of viral pathogens.

Evaluation of Vaccinal Efficacy: You learn how to evaluate the vaccinal efficacy of Marek's disease virus vector vaccines, including experimental design, data collection, and analysis to assess vaccine performance and effectiveness.

Through these learning objectives, you will develop a robust skill set in virology, molecular biology, and vaccine development, contributing to advancements in avian disease prevention and control.

Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Taejoong Kim (taejoong.kim@usda.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: As soon as possible. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Participant Stipend: The participant will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.ARS.Southeast@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a doctoral degree in the one of the relevant fields. 

Preferred skills:

A highly motivated scientist in the virology and vaccine development 
Strong hands-on techniques in DNA/RNA amplification, molecular cloning, transgene gene expression, virus propagation, cell cultures

Description
About Texas A&M AgriLife
Texas A&M AgriLife is comprised of the following Texas A&M University System members:
• Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service
• Texas A&M AgriLife Research
• College of Agriculture and Life Sciences at Texas A&M University
• Texas A&M Forest Service
• Texas A&M Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory

As the nation’s largest most comprehensive agriculture program, Texas A&M AgriLife brings together a college and four state agencies focused on agriculture and life sciences within The Texas A&M University System. With over 5,000 employees and a presence in every county across the state, Texas A&M AgriLife is uniquely positioned to improve lives, environments and the Texas economy through education, research, extension and service.

Click here to learn more about how you can be a part of AgriLife and make a difference in the world!

Position Information:
Texas A&M AgriLife Research seeks an innovative, collaborative, and highly motivated scientist to serve as an Assistant Professor in Precision Ranching. This is a 12-month, 100% research appointment administratively housed at the Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center in San Angelo, Texas, with strong preference for the candidate to be based primarily at the Texas A&M AgriLife Sonora Experiment Station, where the proposed faculty member will engage closely with regional stakeholders to address their needs through research. The successful candidate will hold an affiliation with either the Department of Rangeland, Wildlife & Fisheries Management or the Department of Biological and Agricultural Engineering at Texas A&M University.
The successful candidate will develop a nationally recognized, externally funded research program focused on advancing the productivity, profitability, and sustainability of rangeland systems through the application of precision technologies, data-driven decision support tools, and integrated resource management strategies. The position will foster interdisciplinary collaborations across Texas A&M AgriLife Research, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service, Texas A&M University, industry partners, and other stakeholder groups.

Texas rangelands comprise approximately 60% of the state's land area and support livestock production, wildlife habitat, water resources, recreation, agritourism, and numerous ecosystem services. This position will address emerging challenges and opportunities through the application of smart sensing technologies, remote monitoring systems, automation, artificial intelligence, and advanced analytics to improve management decisions and resource stewardship across rangeland enterprises.

Responsibilities:
Develop and maintain an externally funded, nationally recognized research program addressing
critical challenges facing Texas rangeland and livestock industries.
Conduct fundamental, applied, and translational research focused on precision ranching
technologies and management systems.
Advance innovative solutions related to:
Rangeland restoration and management.
Livestock production efficiency and resource optimization.
Smart sensing, automation, and digital agriculture technologies.
Wildfire mitigation and invasive species management.
Watershed management and water quality protection.
Integrated multi-enterprise ranching systems, including agritourism.
Publish research findings in high-impact peer-reviewed journals and other relevant outlets.
Mentor graduate students and supervise research personnel.
Secure competitive extramural funding from federal, state, industry, and private sources.
Collaborate with AgriLife Research and Extension faculty, industry stakeholders, government agencies, and nonprofit organizations.
Translate research outcomes into practical applications that support stakeholder adoption and economic impact.
Contribute to intellectual property development, technology transfer, and stakeholder engagement activities.

Administrative Relationships:
Reports to the Center Director, Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center at San Angelo with academic guidance provided by the affiliated department.
Provides direction and supervision for research personnel, support staff, and graduate students associated with the program.

Qualifications:
Required job qualifications:
Ph.D. in Rangeland Science, Biological and Agricultural Engineering, or a closely related discipline by the date of appointment.
Expertise in rangeland production systems and management practices.
Demonstrated experience with precision agriculture technologies, smart sensor systems, remote sensing, data analytics, automation, or related technologies.
Record of publishing original research in peer-reviewed journals.
Strong written, verbal, and interpersonal communication skills.

Preferred job qualifications:
Demonstrated experience with range plant identification and field-based vegetation sampling.
Prior academic, post-doctoral, or professional research experience.
Demonstrated ability to secure competitive external funding.
Experience working with federal agencies or in other multi-agency collaborative settings.
Ability to build collaborative and multidisciplinary research programs.
Ability to communicate and build relationships with regional stakeholders to identify needs to address through research.

Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities:
Knowledge of rangeland production systems and management practices in semi-arid rangelands, including strong plant identification skills and experience with field sampling methods.
Strong project management and organizational skills.
Demonstrated leadership and team-building capabilities.
Ability to manage multiple projects and priorities effectively.
Professional judgment, initiative, and interpersonal effectiveness.
Understanding of the mission and role of the Land-Grant University System.

A minimum of four years of experience is required, inclusive of PhD education.

Location and Facilities:
Texas A&M AgriLife’s San Angelo Research and Extension Center is an off-campus center located in San Angelo, Texas, known for its long history of work on small ruminant ranching, rangelands and wildlife in the West Central Texas region. Scientists at the center conduct research on site and at satellite stations located in Crockett, Edwards, Sutton, and Menard counties, totaling about 15,000 acres. Each location has all the equipment required for managing the livestock on these properties including cross fencing, corrals, livestock scales, barns, and storage facilities.

Sonora Station (Sutton and Edwards counties) recently celebrated its 110th anniversary as a research facility. Sonora Station totals 3,300 acres, located about 27 miles south of Sonora, Texas. Research at Sonora Station has covered all facets of rangelands, including small ruminant management and production, grazing systems, water management, prescribed fire and grazing with goats to reduce juniper invasion for savanna restoration, wildlife ecology, and rangeland plant ecology to name a few. Datasets from some of these projects span decades to inform and support future work. In addition to Sonora Station, the San Angelo Center also manages two other Texas A&M AgriLife Research ranches where similar research is conducted. Read Ranch (Crockett County) totals about 5,000 acres located near Ozona, Texas and the Carl and Bina Sue Martin Ranch totals about 4,700 acres located near Menard, Texas.

The successful candidate will have opportunities to conduct research across the properties associated with the center and collaborate extensively across Texas A&M AgriLife, other universities, governmental agencies, industry partners, and nonprofit organizations to develop impactful research programs that address regional, national, and global challenges in rangeland management and precision livestock systems. These activities will support the missions and strategic plans of the San Angelo Research and Extension Center and Texas A&M AgriLife Research.

Additional information about Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center at San Angelo, the Department of Rangeland, Wildlife & Fisheries Management, and the Department of Biological and Agricultural Engineering and Texas A&M University is available at:
• Texas A&M AgriLife Research
• Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center, San Angelo
• Texas A&M University Department of Rangeland, Wildlife & Fisheries Management
• Texas A&M University Department of Biological and Agricultural Engineering

Why Work at Texas A&M AgriLife?
When you choose to work for Texas A&M AgriLife, you become part of an organization that is an established leader in agriculture and life sciences with a wide range of capabilities to meet the needs of our statewide, national, and international constituents.

In addition, Texas A&M AgriLife offers a comprehensive benefit package including the following:

Description: Dr. Stuart Ludsin (https://u.osu.edu/ludsinlab/) is seeking a post-doctoral scientist to help on a Great Lakes Fishery Commission project designed to develop a novel data-sharing platform to advance research and scientific endeavors in support of ecosystem-based fisheries management in the Great Lakes Basin. The post-doc will be expected to conduct structured or semi-structured interviews, create and analyze data from surveys, and organize workshops involving fishery managers, academic and agency researchers, and fishing groups. The post-doc would also work with an interdisciplinary team of scientists and computer/data engineers to develop a prototype of this data-sharing platform, which would allow end-users  (e.g., academic and agency researchers, fishery managers) to simultaneously query existing, independent Great Lakes databases and download their needed data in the proper spatial and temporal resolution through a user-friendly online interface (see next page for an overview). Beyond these activities, the post-doc will be expected to write and submit manuscripts for publication to peer-reviewed journals, help generate scientific proposals, give presentations in management and scientific settings, and help generate annual progress reports to the Great Lakes Fishery Commission, which is this project’s sponsor. 

Funding exists for at least one year, with the possibility of extension for additional years. The ideal start time is late fall/winter 2026-2027.

Qualifications: Required qualifications include: (1) a PhD in social science, data science, computer science, information systems, environmental science, ecology, or related field; (2) demonstrated ability to conduct independent human dimensions research, as evidenced by peer-reviewed publications; and (3) strong written and oral communication skills, including the ability and desire to interact with Great Lakes stakeholders (e.g., managers, fishing groups) and researchers. While knowledge of database/data-sharing platform development and associated programming could prove beneficial, it is not required. 

Salary: $62,232 - $70,000 annually, depending on experience, plus a comprehensive benefits package.

Location: Successful candidates would join a dynamic, interactive group of faculty, post-docs, and students at the Aquatic Ecology Laboratory (AEL; http://ael.osu.edu/) in the Department of Evolution, Ecology, and Organismal Biology (http://eeob.osu.edu/) on The Ohio State University’s main (Columbus) campus. Computing support and office space would be available in the AEL. Working on location in Columbus is preferred. 

How to apply: Submit to apps.ael@gmail.comin a single .pdf file: 1) a cover letter highlighting your research background and interests; 2) a full CV; and 3) names and contact information of three references. Please include “Data-sharing Platform Post-doc” and your last name in the subject line.

Application review will begin immediately and continue until a suitable candidate is found. Questions about the position can be addressed to Stuart Ludsin (ludsin.1@osu.edu).

 The Ohio State University is an equal opportunity employer, including veterans and disability.

Contact
Stuart Ludsin
6147957044
ludsin.1@osu.edu (preferred contact method)

USDA Forest Service Office/Lab and Location: A fellowship opportunity is available with the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Forest Service (FS) within the Pacific Northwest Research Station (PNWRS) located in Hilo, Hawaii.

At the heart of the USDA Forest Service's mission is their purpose. Everything they do is intended to help sustain forests and grasslands for present and future generations. Why? Because their stewardship work supports nature in sustaining life. This is the purpose that drives the agency’s mission and motivates their work across the agency. It’s been there from the agency’s very beginning, and it still drives them. To advance the mission and serve their purpose, the USDA Forest Service balances the short and long-term needs of people and nature by: working in collaboration with communities and our partners; providing access to resources and experiences that promote economic, ecological, and social vitality; connecting people to the land and one another; and delivering world-class science, technology and land management.

The USDA Forest Service Pacific Southwest Research Station’s Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry (IPIF), based in Hawai'i, leads research that supports healthy forests, resilient ecosystems, and sustainable land management across the Pacific region. IPIF focuses on issues such as invasive species, forest health, climate resilience, native habitat restoration, and community-based stewardship. More information is available at: https://www.fs.usda.gov/research/psw/programs/ipif

Research Project: This project supports a broader effort to strengthen invasive-species detection and protect Pacific Island ecosystems. You will gain hands-on experience developing and testing practical methods for identifying coconut rhinoceros beetles in materials like green waste, mulch, compost, and nursery plants. Activities may include helping collect and organize field samples, preparing materials for detection trials, helping with evaluations of trained detection dogs, and contributing to comparisons between different inspection approaches. You will also help with field testing at partner facilities, gather feedback from stakeholders, and support the creation of clear guidance and training materials. You will also have opportunities to explore a wide range of conservation and applied research projects at USDA Forest Service Pacific Southwest Research Station’s Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry, including work in forest health, invasive species, ecosystem restoration, and native habitat conservation across Hawai‘i and the Pacific.

Learning Objectives: 

Detail methods for detecting coconut rhinoceros beetles in green waste, mulch, compost, nursery plants, and other high-risk materials.
Evaluate field samples for invasive-species detection trials.
Differentiate different inspection and screening approaches, including comparisons of their effectiveness and feasibility.
Contribute to clear guidance documents, training materials, and recommendations for agencies and partners.
Understand how invasive-species detection supports forest health, agricultural protection, ecosystem restoration, and conservation of culturally important resources across Hawai‘i and the Pacific.
Mentor: The mentor for this opportunity is Kealohanuiopuna Kinney (kealohanuiopuna.m.kinney@usda.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: October 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year but may be extended upon recommendation of USDA Forest Service and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full-time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and USDA Forest Service. Participants do not become employees of USDA, USDA Forest Service, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process please email  ORISE.USFS.PSWRS@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received an associate's degree in the one of the relevant fields.

Preferred skills:

Academic experience in natural resources, biology, ecology, forestry, environmental science, or a related field. Coursework with a basic understanding of ecological systems, species identification, environmental processes, and scientific data collection. Education that includes both field and laboratory components, along with introductory experience using GPS, GIS, or other mapping tools.
Familiarity with plant, tree, or wildlife identification
Experience using common field tools and basic navigation equipment.
Comfort being outdoors in variable conditions and hiking across uneven terrain
Experience with GIS, digital data systems

 Organizational Mission: 

The Appalachian Trail Conservancy’s mission is to protect, manage, and advocate for the Appalachian National Scenic Trail.

Position Summary
The Education Coordinator will report to the Regional Manager and will support registered thru-hikers and provide education on Leave No Trace, local rules & regulations, proper food storage, and other pertinent information. The Education Coordinator works primarily at the designated basecamp and will work with ATC staff and trail club volunteers. This role will help ensure consistent educational messaging, capacity for important food storage demonstrations, and better balance of shared duties with volunteers.

Volunteers will continue to help assist at the designated basecamp location and provide primary coverage during the coordinators off days. This role will have positive educational conversations and help prevent a cascade of negative effects on natural resources and the trail that would otherwise reach not only the specific region, but the rest of the Appalachian Trail.   

Essential Duties and Responsibilities
Facilitate Start Smart video presentations for registered thru-hikers and answer visitor questions with a Leave No Trace focus in messaging.   
Participate in weekly check-in calls with all stakeholders including ATC partners, volunteers, and internal staff.  
Update messaging focus boards based on information from partners.  
Demonstrate PCT-style hangs when requested.  
Ensure ATC’s Incident Report and Bear Encounter Report Forms are shared with visitors.  
Coordinate with designated Trail Ambassador Coordinator on coverage at basecamp. •           Troubleshoot technology issues as they arise from digital tablet registration   
Ensure good communication with park service on needs for the AT.  
Other duties as assigned by the Regional Manager. 
Qualifications
Academic experience or course work in environmental studies, recreation management, natural resources management, forestry, or related field preferred. 
Commitment to ATC management and resource protection efforts. 
Proven ability to work with minimal supervision. 
Ability to effectively communicate with individuals, groups, and partners. 
Ability to live independently and work in a remote area with minimal supervision. 
Strong hiking and outdoor experience. 
Experience in collaborating with volunteers of all ages, backgrounds, and skill levels. 
Basic knowledge of Appalachian Trail Conservancy’s cooperative management system preferred. 
Leave No Trace Trainer or Master Educator desirable, awareness training is provided. 
Current Wilderness First-Aid, or higher, and CPR certification is preferred training is provided. 
Willingness to participate in additional required training which includes but not limited to: USFS chainsaw & crosscut saw certification, WFR/WFA, advanced rockwork, rigging, safe driving. 
Physical Demands and Work Environment
Must be able to hike for extended periods and perform routine moderate lifting carrying up to 50 pounds in a backpack over a minimum of five miles through rough, uneven terrain, and wet, and slippery surfaces. 
Possible exposure to ticks and pests, extreme weather, and hazards typical of a backcountry environment. 
Regular use of a computer is required; Microsoft Office, Office 365, ESRI GIS, NPS database, APD, NetSuite, RIMS, and Google applications are used. 
Must have a valid driver’s license, and access to a reliable personal vehicle. 
Additional Details:

12-week season beginning in early February and finishing at the end of April.
In-person training will begin Monday February 1st, 2027. Any remote training components that take place prior to the in-person training will be communicated ahead of time. 
The last day of the season will be Monday April 19th, 2027.
Up to $500/month housing stipend available if needed.

Description
Ongoing monitoring of free-roaming cheetahs within a 27,000-hectare (66,700-acre) nature reserve in Limpopo, South Africa, provides a basis for investigating their movements and population ecology. By combining photographic records and spatial information, the project contributes to our understanding of how individual cheetahs use the landscape and how their movements and activity patterns change over time.

Research Focus:
Monitoring cheetahs through camera trap surveys
Identifying individual animals from distinctive coat patterns
Maintaining and expanding photographic identification records
Recording locations and movements to investigate spatial use of the reserve
Examining patterns in habitat use, activity, and distribution
Processing and interpreting data collected through ongoing monitoring

Working with a long-term dataset allows interns to contribute to an ongoing monitoring programme while developing a practical understanding of cheetah ecology. The information collected can help track individuals over time and provide valuable insight into how cheetahs move through and utilise a dynamic bushveld landscape.

Interns will gain practical experience in wildlife identification, camera trap monitoring, field data collection, spatial ecology, and ecological data analysis. The project combines fieldwork with data management and interpretation, providing valuable experience in applied carnivore research and conservation.

Ideal Candidates:
Students or recent graduates with a background in biology, ecology, zoology, wildlife management, or a related discipline
A strong interest in carnivore ecology and wildlife conservation
Comfortable working outdoors
Observant and methodical, with an interest in animal identification
Able to work independently while contributing positively to a research team

Internship Duration
The minimum duration is 2 months.

Conservation Fees & Logistics
Please note that a monthly conservation fee applies, which includes:

Support for ongoing conservation initiatives
Shared accommodation within the reserve in a fenced research camp
Transport (Polokwane airport pick-up/drop-off and fortnightly town trips)

How to Apply
Submit your CV to applications@bushveldbiodiversity.org 

If you’re interested but unavailable on the listed dates, please still submit your resume—we can discuss alternative dates based on our project schedule.

SUMMARY:

The Arkansas Game and Fish Commission (AGFC) Conservation Program Biologist II (FISHERIES DIVISION) is responsible for supervising a fisheries management resource. This position is governed by state and federal laws and agency/institution policy.

TYPICAL FUNCTIONS:

Supervises a small to medium-sized professional staff by interviewing, recommending hire or termination, assigning and reviewing work, evaluating employee performance, and training employees
Addresses program, district, hatchery, and divisional administrative duties
Directs the planning, preparation, and implementation of projects on Arkansas’ streams, rivers, reservoirs, and fish culture facilities.
Develops aquatic species conservation plans, aquatic species management plans, stream and river management plans, and reservoir management plans.
Coordinates and leads biological surveys and studies of aquatic fauna, determining vital rate functions that shape population structure and condition. 
Statistically analyzes data, writes summary reports, and publishes peer-reviewed journal articles.
Coordinates the gathering of public input through public meetings, angler creel surveys, and other survey methods.
Communicates regularly with the appropriate assistant chief and/or fisheries district coordinators regarding oversight for budgets, contracts, and grants.
Develops and maintains program, district, or hatchery budgets.
Serves on internal working groups, as well as external statewide, regional, and national working groups and teams.
Coordinates public relations work with various agencies, private industry, professional and civic organizations, and outdoor recreational groups.
Must understand and be willing to function in a multi-faceted, team-oriented work environment.  
Must maintain close individual contact with and develop solid working relationships with all Fisheries Division, agency, and partner organization personnel
Performs other duties as assigned.

SPECIFIC JOB DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES:

As an AGFC District Fisheries Supervisor (Conservation Program Biologist II), you will join a highly trained, progressive team of fisheries scientists working to improve conservation and management of aquatic resources in Arkansas. You will receive outstanding training and competitive pay and benefits, and will be responsible for fisheries management activities within a district, with opportunities to collaborate on projects throughout the state.

Job duties include:

•Standardized fish population surveys
•Onsite and offsite angler surveys
•Stakeholder engagement
•Fish habitat improvement projects and analysis of survey data
•Preparation of annual fishery sample report management plans
•All district administrative duties
•Fishing access development
•Working with other agencies and elected officials on improving fisheries resources

This position is located in southwest Arkansas and spans the southern Ouachita Mountains and western South Central Plains ecoregions. Fisheries resources are abundant and include: the Red, Cossatot, Little Missouri, and Saline rivers, as well as lakes Millwood, Dierks, DeQueen, Gillham, Bois D'Arc, and Mercer Bayou. This position works under the supervision of the Fisheries District Coordinator in the Management Section of the Fisheries Division 

KNOWLEDGE, ABILITIES, AND SKILLS:

•Knowledge of the principles of biology, ecology, and related environmental sciences
•Knowledge of fisheries principles and techniques
•Knowledge of laboratory and field survey equipment, techniques, and procedures
•Knowledge of supervisory practices and procedures
•Knowledge of state purchasing procedures
•Ability to plan work unit objectives and operational activities and to assign and direct the work of subordinates
•Ability to make public presentations
•Ability to plan and direct scientific surveys and studies
•Ability to develop, implement, and monitor fisheries plans and programs

PREFERRED KNOWLEDGE, ABILITIES, AND SKILLS:

•Knowledge of fish population dynamics, population simulation modeling, and common statistical analysis
•Skill in working with the public
•Experience in current fish sampling techniques
•Good written and verbal communication skills
•Physically able to work long hours, sometimes under harsh or physically demanding conditions
•Strong teamwork skills, yet capable of completing a task without close supervision
•Strong organizational skills.

MINIMUM EDUCATION AND/OR EXPERIENCE:

The formal education equivalent of a bachelor's degree in biology, ecology, fisheries management, or a related field; plus three years of experience in fisheries or a related field, including one year in a leadership capacity.

OTHER JOB-RELATED EDUCATION AND/OR EXPERIENCE MAY BE SUBSTITUTED FOR ALL OR PART OF THESE BASIC REQUIREMENTS, EXCEPT FOR CERTIFICATION OR LICENSURE REQUIREMENTS, UPON APPROVAL OF THE HUMAN RESOURCES CHIEF.

PREFERRED MINIMUM EDUCATION AND/OR EXPERIENCE:
 
A master's degree in fisheries management is strongly preferred.

SPECIAL JOB DIMENSIONS:

Frequent in-state travel and fieldwork with exposure to inclement weather are required.

CERTIFICATES, LICENSES, REGISTRATIONS:

Must possess a valid Arkansas driver’s license.

Class A CDL may be required based on job duties assigned. Must acquire and maintain professional accreditation in the area of expertise.

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION:

All applicants are subject to a criminal background check.

For questions or additional information on the position, please contact Sean Lusk, Fisheries District Coordinator, at email: sean.lusk@agfc.ar.gov or by phone: 501-802-1112.
